title_en: ChatGPT for Teens is an ‘unacceptable risk,’ says Common Sense Media

excerpt_en: Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that offers reviews of apps, services, and entertainment with a focus on youth safety, today said that OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens is an "unacceptable risk." ChatGPT for Teens, introduced in August, has guardrails for teens and is designed to help...

content_en:
Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that offers reviews of apps, services, and entertainment with a focus on youth safety, today said that OpenAI’s ChatGPT for Teens is an “unacceptable risk.”
ChatGPT for Teens is an ‘unacceptable risk,’ says Common Sense Media
ChatGPT’s teen-focused experience ‘doesn’t send alerts to parents when it should,’ according to an assessment.
ChatGPT’s teen-focused experience ‘doesn’t send alerts to parents when it should,’ according to an assessment.
ChatGPT for Teens, introduced in August, has guardrails for teens and is designed to help students learn, but Common Sense Media says that the teen protections offered by the feature “fall short of what the company promised.” Common Sense Media’s assessment found that ChatGPT “doesn’t send alerts to parents when it should,” doesn’t offer “the right help in crisis situations,” and “still does kids’ homework,” according to a press release.
“ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails and safety alerts that frequently don’t work,” Tom Siegel, the executive director of Common Sense Media’s Youth AI Safety Institute, says in a statement. “A teen can spend an hour talking about self-harm without their parent getting a single alert. Until OpenAI fixes that and proves it with independent testing, ChatGPT should be for adults only.” You can read the full assessment here.
OpenAI is pushing back on the assessment. Here’s a statement from OpenAI spokesperson Eric Porterfield:
We are deeply committed to teen safety and to developing safeguards and giving parents meaningful tools to guide their teens’ use of AI. We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media’s testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT’s teen safeguards work in practice or expert perspectives on how AI can support teens. Our review of Common Sense Media’s methodology shows that the bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete, making their findings inaccurate. If that was the case, the tests would not establish whether parental safety notifications work as designed.
We are committed to continuing to work with experts to ensure our products provide teens opportunities to learn and create and give parents confidence.
I shared OpenAI’s statement with Common Sense Media, and here’s Siegel’s response:
We stand behind our testing methodology and our results. Before we began testing, we confirmed with OpenAI that Teen mode features such as eating disorder notifications and study mode were fully launched.
For one of the features we evaluated — parental notifications — OpenAI disclosed after our tests that its systems can take several hours to activate on newly linked accounts. Some of our test accounts were linked within that window; however, others were linked for significantly longer, and still provided no notifications. This new information does not change our conclusion that parental alerts are unreliable for crisis situations.
Prior to release, we shared our evaluation results with OpenAI in good faith to allow it to improve its product. Keeping kids safe requires rigorous independent evaluations like ours, and we hope OpenAI will engage on the substance of what we found, rather than trying to sow doubt on our methodology.

title_en: Apple TV's F1 coverage will now support Dolby Atmos
title_fa: Apple TV's F1 coverage will now support Dolby Atmos
excerpt_en: Apple TV's F1 coverage will feature Dolby Atmos support, starting with the US Grand Prix in Texas later this month.
excerpt_fa: Apple TV's F1 coverage will feature Dolby Atmos support, starting with the US Grand Prix in Texas later this month.
content_en:
Apple TV’s F1 coverage will now support Dolby Atmos
The upgraded audio will debut at the US Grand Prix in Austin later this month.
Apple TV's Formula 1 coverage will support Dolby Atmos, starting with the US Grand Prix in Austin, Texas taking place from October 22 through October 25. Last year, Apple scored the exclusive deal for the US broadcast rights to Formula 1 racing, and its coverage started with the first grand prix weekend earlier this year. The company created a dedicated channel for it in the Apple TV app, where you can watch not just the races themselves, but also practice sessions, sprint races and both pre- and post-race coverage. You'll also have access to onboard cameras, team radios and live telemetry with your Apple TV subscription.
Dolby Atmos delivers spatial sound, making it as if audio is coming from different parts of the room. John Couling, the Senior VP for Entertainment at Dolby Laboratories, told Business of Speed that Apple can use F1's existing trackside microphones and sensors for its Atmos coverage instead of introducing new hardware.
Apple TV's library isn't as expansive as other streaming services yet, and it's also not a massive sports broadcaster, so it doesn't come as a surprise that this is the first time it's introducing Atmos support for a sports offering. Of course, you can only enjoy Dolby Atmos if you have a TV or audio system that supports the technology.

title_en: Spotify expands audiobooks to over 180 markets
title_fa: Spotify expands audiobooks to over 180 markets
excerpt_en: Spotify will make 350,000 titles available in over 120 languages for this expansion
excerpt_fa: Spotify will make 350,000 titles available in over 120 languages for this expansion
content_en:
Spotify announced on Wednesday that it’s expanding audiobook access to over 180 markets worldwide, including regions across Europe, the Americas, the Caribbean, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia. The rollout is starting today and will continue over the coming months. With this move, more than 750 million users will be able to access audiobooks, allowing Spotify to better compete with both music streaming providers and audiobook apps like Audible.
Before this, audiobooks were available primarily in English-speaking markets like the U.S., U.K., Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand, as well as in Germany.
The audio platform said it has more than 350,000 titles for its new markets and has increased its collection to include over 120 languages. With its launch in Spain, users in the country will have access to over 45,000 titles in Spanish.
Spotify is working with more than 300 publishers worldwide, including Planeta and Mondadori, to increase the number of titles available in different markets.
With a Premium subscription, users can listen to 12 hours of audiobooks in eligible countries such as Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, Poland, Chile, Norway, and Peru. People across the world can also purchase an Audiobook+ standalone subscription to get access to titles with a 15-hour allowance. Alternatively, users can buy individual titles directly.
Spotify is also adding an Audiobook+ add-on for student plans in select regions in November. The company said that since its launch last year, Audiobook+ has gained over 1 million subscribers and has fetched over 100 million in annual recurring revenue for the platform.
In February, the company launched a “Page Match” feature, which lets users scan a page of a physical book and find the corresponding point in the audiobook to listen to. Since the launch, 1 million people have been using the feature monthly, the company noted.
Spotify said that over the last year, monthly listeners of audiobooks grew by 40% and listening hours increased by 30%.
This year, the company introduced Audiobook Charts to let people discover popular titles. It also launched an AI-powered tool for authors to turn their books into audiobooks using models from ElevenLabs. Plus, Spotify started experimenting with physical sales of books through its audiobook platform in select markets like the U.S. and the U.K.

title_en: How long have wireless gaming controllers been around for?
title_fa: How long have wireless gaming controllers been around for?
excerpt_en: Game controllers have experimented with losing the cords for longer than you'd think, but early attempts didn't have much success.
excerpt_fa: Game controllers have experimented with losing the cords for longer than you'd think, but early attempts didn't have much success.
content_en:
How long have wireless gaming controllers been around for?
It took a while for controllers to work as well as they do today without cables.
If you've been a gamer for a while, you might know that wireless controllers have been used as far back as the 1980s. Those who grew up in the PS2/Xbox/GameCube era likely have a different gamepad in mind when they think of early wireless controllers. While wireless pads were tried in various iterations over the decades, they were only perfected within the last few console generations.
The history of non-wired controllers is fascinating. Here's the story of how your current console has unleashed you from the couch.
When did controllers first become wireless?
As a 41-year-old, I'm slightly relieved that the first wireless gaming controller is older than me: enter the Cynex Game Mate 2. Released around 1982, this is an Atari 2600 peripheral widely regarded as the first wireless console-compatible gamepad. It was the debut of an evolving, genre-defying tech, albeit one that wouldn't be fully realized for some time to come.
The Game Mate 2 used radio frequencies. By embracing RF technology, this pioneering pad gave gamers more freedom than lesser IR alternatives that would launch later in the decade. Unlike the Acclaim Remote Controller that launched for the NES in 1989, you didn't need to point the Game Mate 2 directly at your Atari 2600 for its signal to be recognized.
Whereas early infrared pads could easily lose signal if any objects came between their sensors and the receiver on the console (much like IR TV remotes), the more flexible Game Mate wasn't bound by these restrictions. Indeed, that early RF tech worked well enough that it reportedly boasted a range of up to 20 feet.
While these were ahead of their time, they weren't perfect. They were weighty and clunky, being essentially a standard 2600 controller on top of a heavy base. They also drained the required 9V battery quickly. Once Atari took over distribution a year after this peripheral launched, it was rebranded as the CX42 Remote Control Wireless Joystick. Catchy, right?
What was the first mainstream wireless controller?
The GameCube's mini discs weren't the only notable part of the console's legacy. The WaveBird wireless controller arrived in 2002 and was the first mainstream wireless pad that wasn't weighed down by tons of compromises. I have vivid memories of waiting in line on a semi-balmy May evening in my native Edinburgh back in 2002 to pick up the Big N's wondrous purple box, then buying the little console's wireless controller around Christmas that same year.
And what a bulky but beloved brute it was; the WaveBird was anything but subtle. Adding serious girth to the GameCube's standard controller, it came with an equally chunky receiver to plug into the sixth-gen console and required you to match a channel with sliders on each. If you have any affection for the best of the GameCube's library, there's a good chance you played some titles with a WaveBird.
Using radio 2.4G frequency tech for the first time in a controller, the WaveBird had a range of around 20 feet at minimum. It's hard to explain what a big deal it was to have a gamepad that untethered you from a console. No longer did you have to precariously perch within six feet of your beloved gaming box. Instead, you could lean back or even move around the room, which was great for multiplayer sessions so everyone didn't have to crowd onto the same couch.
To maximize battery life, the WaveBird didn't have rumble support, but it ran for up to 100 hours on a pair of AA batteries. The freedom it gave you in controlling games paved the way for future gamepads, leading to all the fabulous wireless controllers from Sony, Microsoft and others that have launched over the last quarter-century.
Which PlayStation had the first wireless controller?
Before learning this history, you might have thought that the first wireless gaming controller was a PlayStation product. That's understandable, since Sony has (mostly) dominated the console market since the PS1 arrived stateside back in 1995. As it turns out, Sony's debut wireless peripheral wasn't introduced until the PS3 era. With the benefit of hindsight, we can say it was a bit of a stinker.
The Sixaxis is perhaps the most infamous Sony controller of all time, minus the banana-shaped "Boomerang" prototype PS3 gamepad that never saw the light of day. As the initial controller model for the PS3, the Sixaxis dropped rumble for half-baked, early, never-fully-realized motion controls.
Not long after the Sixaxis debuted in 2006, Phil Harrison said Sony didn't incorporate rumble into Sixaxis not because of a lawsuit over patent rights, but because it was a "last-generation feature." That was a pretty bold (fairly craven) statement, considering Phil was the President of Sony Computer Entertainment Worldwide Studios at the time.
Although PS3 launch title Resistance: Fall of Man was among the first games to support Sixaxis features, it was really the dragon-riding Lair that came to define the controller. It was widely panned for its semi-botched motion controls, and folks made it clear that the lack of rumble was unacceptable. Sony quickly saw sense, and soon enough, titles like 2007's Ratchet & Clank Future: Tools of Destruction would embrace the palm-shaking possibilities of the DualShock 3 after its 2008 release.

title_en: How to help stop spam calls on iPhone and Android
title_fa: How to help stop spam calls on iPhone and Android
excerpt_en: Spam calls don't have to grab your attention and waste your time. Use these built-in options to silence and block them without having to pay.
excerpt_fa: Spam calls don't have to grab your attention and waste your time. Use these built-in options to silence and block them without having to pay.
content_en:
How to help stop spam calls on iPhone and Android
Spam calls are apparently here to stay, but you have ways to fight back.
Spam calls should be a bygone concern, but unfortunately they're still a plague many of us deal with. Services like Truecaller have helped with caller identification and spam filtering for years. But since Android and iOS have gotten great at handling spam calls on their own, you don't need to rely on a third-party app — much less pay a subscription — to avoid unwanted callers.
In addition to functions on your phone, your carrier may offer its own spam protection features. Depending on the company, these might be enabled by default. If not, check your online account or the carrier's app for a spam protection toggle.
Filtering unwanted calls on iPhone
If you have an iPhone, navigate to Settings > Apps > Phone. The most important option is under the Call Filtering section; enable Spam and calls that your carrier identifies as junk won't ring. They'll be automatically sent to voicemail, and in the Phone app's Calls tab, they appear under the Spam section (accessible under the top-right button).
To further keep your call logs tidy, enable the Unknown Callers option in the same Settings box. With this, recent calls from non-contacts appear under the Unknown Callers section (available via the mentioned top-right button in the Phone app). Use Mark as Known to remove a given number from this section if needed.
Back on the Settings page, review the Screen Unknown Callers section, where you have three options. Never is the default, where every incoming call rings normally. The most aggressive approach is Silence, which mutes all incoming calls from numbers not saved in your contacts and sends them to voicemail. You can view these silenced calls on the same Calls tab of the Phone app.
Ask Reason for Calling is a good middle ground; with this, your iPhone will screen unknown callers and ask them why they're calling. You're able to view a live transcript of the caller's response on your screen and decide whether the call is worth answering. Call Screening is only available in select countries on iPhones running iOS 26 or newer.
While you presumably have friends and family saved in your contacts already, make sure to save any other numbers that contact you regularly, like doctors' offices or work clients. These options are great for shutting up spammers, but you'll need to be a little more vigilant to avoid missing legitimate calls from unsaved numbers.
Managing spam calls on Android
Most Android phones offer spam detection for calls, although availability and capabilities vary depending on your phone's model, its Android version and the dialer app you use. The official Phone app by Google is what most Android manufacturers ship with their devices, and it comes with caller ID and spam detection built-in. If your phone uses a different dialer, poke through its settings to look for a similar solution, or download Google's Phone app and set it as the default dialer.
Launch the Phone app, tap the hamburger menu (three horizontal lines) at the top-left and choose Settings. Under the Call Assist section, tap Caller ID and spam. Here, enable See caller and spam ID to have the app warn you of an incoming potential spam call before you answer it. To go further, enable Filter spam calls to automatically silence suspected junk calls.
You can still view missed calls and voicemails from unknown callers in the Phone app. For both of these features to work, you'll need a phone running Android 6.0 or newer, with the latest version of the Phone app by Google installed and set as the default.
Some Android phones, including ones from Samsung and Google, feature enhanced call screening options akin to the Ask Reason for Calling feature on iPhone. If you own a Pixel 6 or newer, launch the Phone app and navigate to Settings > Spam and Call Screen > Call Screen to set up this feature. On supported Samsung phones, open the Phone app, tap the three-dot icon in the top-right corner and navigate to Settings > Call screening.

OpenAI has revealed solutions to a number of long-standing mathematics problems produced by an unreleased frontier model in a batch of 722 manuscripts, covering 372 result families that group related papers. It extends a run of breakthroughs that have both impressed and unsettled parts of the mathematical community while raising questions about research ethics and academic conduct. According to AGMAI, the newly formed independent advisory group of elite mathematicians put together to work on communicating the results responsibly, the release includes solutions to “hundreds” of open questions.
OpenAI drops another batch of mathematical breakthroughs
Solutions to ‘hundreds’ of open questions are said to be included in a batch of manuscripts released by OpenAI.
Solutions to ‘hundreds’ of open questions are said to be included in a batch of manuscripts released by OpenAI.
The results have been expected for weeks, although until now OpenAI had not provided details about which problems the model had solved or exactly when they would be published. In September, the company said its model had “resolved more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics.” The released papers and other details also include some summaries of the model’s reasoning, estimates of the compute used, and stats about the number of problems attempted. OpenAI claims the “average result” used the equivalent of three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking.
AGMAI, or the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, published its first recommendations in late September, urging AI labs to release mathematical results promptly and through established academic channels where possible, while disclosing details such as the name of the model used, prompts, and compute costs. The group also implored AI companies to “refrain from treating the release of mathematical results as marketing vehicles to promote their models,” a practice they said inflicts significant harm on the mathematical community.
Here’s how OpenAI described its process for this release:
For this release, we’re publishing the results in a GitHub repository, with protocols for paper revisions and citations. We’re continuing to explore other community-hosted alternatives for this release which meet the committee’s guidelines. For future releases, we are committed to further improving the quality of the papers via the citations, mathematical exposition, and presentation of the results for better understanding
The full impact of the results will likely take some time to be felt as mathematicians assess and digest them. They add to a rapidly growing body of mathematical results from OpenAI and rival labs like Anthropic that the field is still processing, including results concerning a Millennium Prize problem, among the most famous open questions in the field. The speed at which AI labs have barreled into the discipline this year — particularly their handling of announcements — has provoked fierce debate over research practices, ethics, and how companies credit the human mathematicians whose work their systems build upon and potentially use to produce results.

title_en: Why do some PCs have two Ethernet ports?
title_fa: Why do some PCs have two Ethernet ports?
excerpt_en: Dual Ethernet ports don't automatically provide faster speed, but they increase your networking options.
excerpt_fa: Dual Ethernet ports don't automatically provide faster speed, but they increase your networking options.
content_en:
Why do some PCs have two Ethernet ports?
Your PC probably doesn’t need both ports, but workstations and servers can put them to work.
The two Ethernet ports on some PCs aren't a matter of aesthetics or a simple selling point. Their primary purpose is to provide the computer with more networking options, like backup connections or separate networks. If it's configured for failover and you lose a network connection on one, you still have access through the other. In most cases, it's a feature that's primarily relevant for workstations, servers or virtualization setups. Your home internet likely doesn't go out often enough to justify paying for a second connection you only need when the first is unavailable.
Dual ports can also support link aggregation (sometimes called NIC teaming or bonding). Put simply, link aggregation allows the PC (and a managed switch, in some setups) to combine two Ethernet links into a single connection. This has the added benefit of boosting bandwidth while maintaining the aforementioned redundancy.
Don't expect two Ethernet to magically double your internet plan; you're not going from 1 Gbps down to 2 Gbps. Link aggregation has to be supported and configured on both ends, and while you can share the extra capacity, data transfer generally remains limited to the speed of one link.
Keep networks separate
The most useful benefit of two Ethernet ports is network versatility, especially with everything Ethernet cables can do. For example, one port can connect to your regular home network, while the other can connect to a local network (like industrial equipment in a laboratory) or a dedicated storage drive. It's a good method for separating traffic for security purposes or to boost performance.
You can use this feature to turn a small PC into a router or run virtual machines. Virtualization software can assign each virtual machine to a specific Ethernet port, allowing one VM to use a certain network while the PC uses another. While Ethernet cables still have limits, having two Ethernet ports open the door to a more efficient workplace or workflow, especially for those working in cybersecurity, network administration or running a small business server.
For a desktop PC at home, something the family uses or a gaming setup, the additional port is more of a nice addition. It's useful if you have a specific need for it, but not necessarily a must-have option.
Will two Ethernet cables slow internet speed?
Using both ports at the same time won't inherently slow down or speed up an internet connection. Just connecting two Ethernet cables into the back of your PC won't boost or drop anything, except for your workflow potential. Without setting it up correctly for a specific purpose, it could even cause connection issues. Link aggregation exists specifically for grouping multiple links safely.
For most home PCs, a single Ethernet port is all you will ever need. Alone, it will provide the stable, wired connection you expect and is generally a better option than a wireless connection. If you have a second Ethernet port, reserve it for something specific like large file transfers to a NAS or home media server.
It's not an extra outlet for simply adding more wired devices to your home network. If your router is out of ports, use an Ethernet switch instead.

title_en: How to find out if Amazon thinks you have ‘flat buttocks’
title_fa: How to find out if Amazon thinks you have ‘flat buttocks’
excerpt_en: "I stumbled upon a page of assumptions that Amazon has made about me based on my purchases and I’m literally speechless," one shopper wrote on Threads.
excerpt_fa: "I stumbled upon a page of assumptions that Amazon has made about me based on my purchases and I’m literally speechless," one shopper wrote on Threads.
content_en:
It shouldn’t come as a surprise that Amazon collects data about you based on what you buy. If you buy a lot of cat litter, Amazon will probably infer that you have cats, or if you buy a lot of anti-acne skin products, then Amazon might guess you’re prone to breakouts. Even if we know that Amazon customizes our shopping experiences based on our purchase history, it still comes as a surprise to see all of these personal details laid out in a convenient list. Especially when those details get uncomfortably intimate.
One Threads user came across this section of her Amazon settings where you can see who the shopping giant thinks you are, and alongside more benign assumptions like “Shops from women’s departments” and “Probably owns a Shark robot vacuum,” she found that Amazon assumes she “has flat buttocks.”
“I stumbled upon a page of assumptions that Amazon has made about me based on my purchases and I’m literally speechless,” an Amazon customer, @fangirlinmegan, wrote on Threads. “I mean it ain’t wrong but damn did you have to call me out like that?”
In less than a day, the post garnered over a million views, including many from users who were curious what their own Amazon profiles might reveal. Here’s how you find out.
On desktop, you can find this page by hovering over where Amazon says “Hello, [your name]” in the upper right corner. Then click “Account” under the “Your Account” section. Under the “Ordering and shopping preferences” section, click “Your Shopping preferences.” From here, you can add in information of your own, like your shoe size, interests, and dietary preferences. But we’re not here to tell Amazon that it should stop selling you beef jerky since you’re a vegetarian. We’re here to see if Amazon thinks you have “flat buttocks.” When you scroll to the bottom of the page, you’ll see a blue hyperlinked option that says “Manage your information.” Once you click that, you’ll see what dirt Amazon has on you.
On the mobile app, you can get here by clicking the hamburger icon from the bottom menu bar, then navigating to Account > Shopping preferences > About you.
For me, Amazon has gleaned that I am someone who “practices photography,” “plays collectible card games,” and is “invested in the Apple ecosystem.” This is all true. Amazon has even flattered me by noting that I “read diverse non-fiction,” to which I say — why yes, I am indeed an open-minded intellectual with a thirst for knowledge. Thank you for noticing.
Other colleagues of mine found that Amazon correctly noted their interests in vinyl records and ceramics, as well as a penchant for “natural materials” in home decor and clothing that “prioritizes comfort.” None of us had anything as affronting as “has flat buttocks,” but the Threads user noted that this was likely because she had purchased “butt scrunch leggings.”
Tech companies know too much about us, and it’s jarring to realize just how closely they’re paying attention to how we use their platforms. We live in a world of alarming surveillance, but at least I know that Amazon doesn’t think my butt is flat.

title_en: Apple is reportedly partnering with LG to launch a smart lock, thermostat, and doorbell
title_fa: Apple is reportedly partnering with LG to launch a smart lock, thermostat, and doorbell
excerpt_en: Apple appears poised to push into the smart home market with a slate of new devices and a key partner.
excerpt_fa: Apple appears poised to push into the smart home market with a slate of new devices and a key partner.
content_en:
Apple is working on a new ecosystem of smart home devices via a partnership with LG, Bloomberg has reported.
The new devices — which include a smart lock, a thermostat, and a doorbell — are designed to integrate with the company’s smart home hub, another upcoming product that will reportedly launch on October 13. That hub is expected to include a 6-inch square display that can be placed on a countertop or mounted on a wall.
The two companies are also working on a slate of security cameras, including models for indoor and outdoor, was well as a floodlight. The LG devices are expected to be announced, if not formally released, next week, too. TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information.
Interestingly, the devices will reportedly carry the LG brand — despite being developed by both companies.
The new products could aptly be read as a swipe at Amazon’s smart home offerings, which currently include a variety of similar products, including its Ring home security cameras.
Apple has sought to push into new territory with its recent hardware releases. One of those new territories is an expanded smart home presence.

title_en: Ex-Ramp engineers raise $20M for platform Melius after scrapping their first product
title_fa: Ex-Ramp engineers raise $20M for platform Melius after scrapping their first product
excerpt_en: Instead of helping marketers manage and optimize ad spend, the company is focusing on building the tools that generate the creative assets and campaigns.
excerpt_fa: Instead of helping marketers manage and optimize ad spend, the company is focusing on building the tools that generate the creative assets and campaigns.
content_en:
Melius, an AI platform for generating ad campaigns, images, and videos, announced on Tuesday that it raised a total of $25 million in funding, including a $20 million Series A led by CRV and a $5 million seed round led by General Catalyst.
While the startup claims to have hit more than $1 million in annualized revenue within two months of coming out of stealth in July, co-founder Joowon Kim (pictured on right) admits that Melius didn’t hit it out of the park initially.
When the New York-based company first launched over a year ago, Kim and his co-founders, Young Kim (pictured on left) and Arnav Ramu (pictured center) set out to build an AI-powered performance marketing tool. The three knew each other from working as engineers at Ramp, the corporate spending and finance software company.
More than six months after building the product, the co-founders decided their original idea didn’t “have legs,” Joowon Kim told TechCrunch.
Instead of helping marketers manage and optimize ad spend, the team chose to focus on what it saw as a much larger opportunity: building the tools that generate the creative assets and campaigns themselves.
“We scrapped the entire codebase; we burned all of it,” Kim said. Melius quickly went to work on an entirely new product. Nearly a year after its initial launch, it revealed a platform that it describes as an “agents lab for creative work.”
Melius is far from the only startup helping ad agencies, marketers, and brands generate creative assets and campaigns with AI. Competitors include rapidly growing Higgsfield, which was valued at $5.4 billion in August, as well as other small startups, including Krea and Flora AI.
Kim isn’t concerned about the competition.
He acknowledged that Higgsfield, a three-year-old company that has hit over $700 million in annualized revenue, “is growing like mad,” but according to Kim, the size of the market is so large that it can support multiple competitors.
“There are a lot of players, which is pretty exciting,” he told TechCrunch. “That means there are customers to be won and there is demand in this space.”
As for why former Ramp engineers are building an ad-generation product, Kim, who describes himself as a social media influencer, says he has been passionate about making short videos since elementary school and once dreamed of becoming a famous YouTuber.
“I tried my best to make vlogs,” he said. “My dad was great at using FinalCut Pro, but I wasn’t.”
Those early vlogs never quite took off, but his fascination with making digital media remained.
Now, with Melius, he’s building the tool he always wanted: a platform where anyone, including seasoned creative directors, can turn their ideas into reality using plain language.

title_en: Apple reportedly worked with LG on gadgets for its upcoming smart home push
title_fa: Apple reportedly worked with LG on gadgets for its upcoming smart home push
excerpt_en: The doorbell, security cameras, thermostats and more could be announced next week.
excerpt_fa: The doorbell, security cameras, thermostats and more could be announced next week.
content_en:
Apple reportedly worked with LG on gadgets for its upcoming smart home push
The doorbell, security cameras, thermostats and more could be announced next week.
We've been hearing a lot about Apple's renewed smart home endeavors from Mark Gurman at Bloomberg over the past few months, and he's back today with a report that the company co-developed several new gadgets in partnership with LG Electronics. Based on recent regulatory filings by LG, Bloomberg reports that the results of this collaboration are expected to include a smart doorbell, a smart thermostat, a smart deadbolt lock, indoor and outdoor security cameras, and a floodlight camera. Rather than Apple's iconic fruit symbol, the hardware will reportedly be sold under LG's banner, with the South Korean business responsible for the devices' manufacturing and product support.
This smart home slate is expected to be unveiled next week, and the LG product lineup is likely to center around a new hub device from Apple that has been in development for several years. A revamped HomePod Mini and TV set-top box may also be coming as part of Apple's move toward offering a bigger system of connected home tech. While the Apple-branded devices are expected to be available soon, Bloomberg says the LG accessories won't hit the market for "at least a few more months."
This co-development effort also marks a shift for LG. The brand has long been known for appliances and large electronics rather than smart home products. LG has been a partner for Apple in other verticals in the past, such offering Apple software via its smart TVs and serving as a third-party monitor option for the MacBook ecosystem. It also produces the panels for Apple's current lineup of Mac monitors, the Studio Display and Studio Display XDR.

title_en: Kindle Click vs Kobo Remote: How much of a difference is there?
title_fa: Kindle Click vs Kobo Remote: How much of a difference is there?
excerpt_en: Of course you're going to get the one that works with your ereader, but which of these page-turning gadgets is actually better?
excerpt_fa: Of course you're going to get the one that works with your ereader, but which of these page-turning gadgets is actually better?
content_en:
Kindle Click vs Kobo Remote: How much of a difference is there?
Wireless and wildly convenient.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Page-turning remotes used to be a niche workaround, something readers cobbled together with third-party clip-on gadgets that tapped the screen on their behalf. Life has changed quite a bit over the past year, as the biggest names in ereaders rolled out official solutions. Rakuten's Kobo got there first with the Kobo Remote and last week, more than a year later, Amazon has introduced the Kindle Click.
Both accessories solve the same basic problem, namely the inconvenience of reaching over to tap your ereader every time you want to turn the page. It can be mildly annoying to do that when you're under the covers with your device mounted to a stand or propped up on the treadmill while you're getting your workout in. A small wireless remote lets you keep your hands wherever they're most comfortable while still reading your story.
On the surface, the Kindle Click and Kobo Remote look like they're solving the same problem in nearly identical ways. Both connect over Bluetooth, both skip the need to physically touch the screen and both come with an optional wrist lanyard. A closer look at pricing, design, battery setup and compatibility reveals some real differences that might matter depending on which ecosystem you're in and what you value in a reading accessory.
Kindle Click
The Kindle Click costs $34.99 and marks Amazon's first entry into the Bluetooth page-turner space. It's a compact remote with two large, equally sized buttons: one for paging forward and one for going back. On the side, there are dedicated buttons that let you adjust the screen brightness without opening a menu, which is quite handy to have. If you press both at the same time, it'll put your Kindle to sleep.
It comes in a single colorway, a boring but classy white with grey buttons. Considering that it's a companion tool to a device that usually gets "dressed" in colorful cases or a gazillion stickers, going for such a simple understated white and gray combo seems like a missed opportunity.
Compatibility is fairly broad. The Click will not only work with the bunch of new Kindle devices that Amazon just launched, but also any Kindle model from 2024 or later. This does mean, though, that older Kindles are left out.
One thing that's extremely convenient about the Kindle Click is that it has a USB-C port so you won't need to swap out any batteries — just plug it in every few weeks, much like you do with your Kindle.
While it's true that at $35, the Click is more expensive than other Bluetooth ereader remotes, it is a lot more convenient to use. The Kindle Click will be released on October 28, but you can pre-order it now.
Kobo Remote
The Kobo Remote was launched back in November 2025 at $29.99 and it was sold out for months due to demand. It's now available at that price on Rakuten's website, but is slightly more expensive at retailers like Target ($31.99) and Amazon($33.99). It comes in both black and white (also a missed opportunity) and connects via Bluetooth, pairing almost instantly and reconnecting automatically whenever a compatible Kobo eReader wakes from sleep. Design-wise, the Kobo Remote brings a more ergonomic model to the table, featuring a 20-degree curve that lets it sit naturally in your hand.
Its two buttons are also shaped differently. One is larger and concave while the other is smaller and convex, so they're easy to tell apart by touch alone. Wireless and wildly convenient.

title_en: Xbox has secured GTA 6 streaming rights
title_fa: Xbox has secured GTA 6 streaming rights
excerpt_en: Xbox CEO Asha Sharma told employees that Microsoft is getting ready to do something around Grand Theft Auto VI that "no other platform holder is doing" during an employee all-hands this morning. According to sources familiar with Microsoft's plans, Sharma's brief teaser was...
excerpt_fa: Xbox CEO Asha Sharma told employees that Microsoft is getting ready to do something around Grand Theft Auto VI that "no other platform holder is doing" during an employee all-hands this morning. According to sources familiar with Microsoft's plans, Sharma's brief teaser was...
content_en:
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma told employees that Microsoft is getting ready to do something around Grand Theft Auto VI that “no other platform holder is doing” during an employee all-hands this morning. According to sources familiar with Microsoft’s plans, Sharma’s brief teaser was actually about Xbox managing to land a deal for game streaming rights for Grand Theft Auto VI.
Xbox has secured GTA 6 streaming rights
The streaming rights come in November, when Microsoft is opening up access to Xbox Cloud Gaming.
The streaming rights come in November, when Microsoft is opening up access to Xbox Cloud Gaming.
The deal will mean Xbox Cloud Gaming can stream Grand Theft Auto VI to players at launch, but it’s not clear how long the agreement will be in place. Rockstar Games still hasn’t announced a PC version of Grand Theft Auto VI, and a streaming deal would normally also allow Xbox to market its Xbox Cloud Gaming service to PC players who would otherwise need an Xbox Series X / S or PS5 console.
After The Verge originally reported that the deal would be exclusive, Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Ball revealed on X that Microsoft wouldn’t be streaming Grand Theft Auto VI exclusively, nor to PCs. That suggests the deal is simply for Xbox console streaming, and may mean the web browsers and apps that can usually access Xbox Cloud Gaming will not be able to stream Grand Theft Auto VI.
News of the streaming rights comes around a month after Microsoft announced some major changes to Xbox Cloud Gaming. From November, the same month Grand Theft Auto VI releases, Microsoft is limiting streaming hours to just 15 hours for Xbox Game Pass Ultimate subscribers, 10 hours for Premium subscribers, and just five hours for Game Pass Essential.
Microsoft is also opening up access to Xbox Cloud Gaming with a pay-as-you-go option next month, rather than being limited to Game Pass subscriptions. The pay-as-you-go option is perfectly timed for Grand Theft Auto VI, allowing those who don’t own an Xbox, or who primarily play from a phone, to stream the game by paying for a bundle of hours.
During the Xbox all-hands, Sharma also told employees that Project Helix, the next generation of Xbox hardware, will be a “family of devices” and that Microsoft will partner with others on some of those devices. Sharma first called Helix a family of devices last month in an interview, after Microsoft and AMD announced a “strategic multi-year partnership” last year to work together on “a portfolio of devices,” including Microsoft’s next-generation Xbox console.
Correction, October 6th: Xbox has clarified that its streaming deal isn’t exclusive and Grand Theft Auto VI won’t be streamed to PCs.

content_en:
Spending too much time constantly sweeping and mopping? If you have the money to delegate those chores to a robot cleaner, you could save a lot of personal time. Thankfully, it’s cheaper than usual to buy a robot vacuum / mop hybrid during Amazon’s Prime Big Deal Days, and some of our favorite models are discounted. The deals aren’t just for Amazon Prime members either, with other retailers like Best Buy and manufacturers getting in on the action, as well.
The best robot vacuum and mop deals during October Prime Day
We spotted deals on some of our favorite robot vacuums and mops from brands like Roborock, Qrevo, and Dreame.
We spotted deals on some of our favorite robot vacuums and mops from brands like Roborock, Qrevo, and Dreame.
That being said, if your floors are already squeaky clean, make sure to check out our roundup of over 100 deals from Amazon’s October sale.
Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow
Roborock’s first roller-mop robot vacuum, the Curv 2 Flow, features flagship specs at a midrange price, including excellent mopping, a retractable mop cover, 20,000Pa suction, AI-powered obstacle avoidance, and a compact design.
Roborock Saros 20
Roborock’s Saros 20 stands out for its ability to climb tall thresholds, avoid obstacles with impressive accuracy, and clean under low furniture thanks to its slim design. It also combines powerful 36,000Pa suction with great spinning mop pads, which is why we recommend it for homes with multiple floor types and tricky transitions between rooms.
Narwal Flow 2
Our pick for the best robot vacuum-mop if you have all hardwood floors is the Narwal Flow 2. A superb mop with a wide flat roller pad and an excellent vacuum, the Flow 2 also has top-notch navigation and obstacle detection. Its sleek base station is also less of an eyesore than most.
Dreame X60 Ultra
The Dreame X60 Ultra leverages a pair of AI-assisted cameras to help it navigate obstacles and ensure a thorough, consistent cleaning. It’s only 3.13 inches tall, so it can sneak under low surfaces that some other robot vacuums can’t.
Eufy Omni C28
The Eufy Omni C28 combines excellent mopping performance with a small self-cleaning dock that’s well suited for apartments and other smaller spaces. It navigates around furniture and into tight areas with ease, while its roller mop does a great job cleaning hard floors.
Dreame L40 Ultra
Dreame’s budget-friendly L40s Ultra has storage for up to 100 days of dust, and can clean its own mop pads. The auxiliary climbing wheels help it navigate thresholds and rug edges with ease.
Roborock Q10 S5 Plus
A budget robot vacuum and mop without a multifunction dock. It has AI-powered obstacle avoidance, sonic mopping, auto mop lifting, and an auto-empty dock.
Best overall: Deebot X8 Pro Omni
The Deebot X8 Pro Omni is an excellent roller mopping bot that extends to clean along backboards and furniture. It’s also a powerful vacuum with great obstacle avoidance, a small dock, and a convenient self-cleaning brush system.
Switchbot K11 Plus
The Matter-compatible SwitchBot K11 Plus is ideal for small apartments, bedrooms, and home offices. It can easily navigate around chair and desk legs and into tight spaces that most other bots miss. It also features a commendable 6,000Pa of suction power — which is great for this price point — and works well on both hardwood and carpet.

title_en: Remember MapQuest? You can now use it with Android Auto
title_fa: Remember MapQuest? You can now use it with Android Auto
excerpt_en: If you use Android Auto, you can try out the beta mapping service today.
excerpt_fa: If you use Android Auto, you can try out the beta mapping service today.
content_en:
Remember MapQuest? You can now use it with Android Auto
If you use Android Auto, you can try out the beta mapping service today.
Launched in 1996, MapQuest, the world's oldest commercially available web mapping service, recently introduced Android Auto support, making it an alternative to Google and Apple Maps with the added distinction of calling a certain body of water in North America Lake Ontario, despite pressure from President Donald Trump.
The decision to retain the lake's 380-year-old name drew a lot of attention. While both Apple and Google bowed to that pressure and changed how the name appears to map users in the US, MapQuest did not. This refusal prompted a huge spike in interest in its service, the company said. Usage grew to 50 times its normal rate, and the apps it offers generated over 1.5 million downloads. MapQuest quickly became the No. 1 mapping app on Apple's App Store. "Hundreds of thousands of people signaled to us this weekend that we got it right, by downloading our app," said Doug Berger, general manager of MapQuest in a statement.
The company is feeding this interest with the introduction of beta support for Android Auto on Google Play.
How to install MapQuest with Android Auto
Using MapQuest with Android Auto is simple:
- Open Google Play on your Android smartphone, find MapQuest, download and install the app, or update it to the latest version if already installed.
- Scroll down the MapQuest page in Google Play, join the beta program and update the app.
- Connect your smartphone to your car in the usual way, using Bluetooth or a compatible USB cable. The MapQuest icon should appear on your dashboard alongside any other mapping services you have installed, such as Google Maps and Waze.
- If it does not, open Settings on your smartphone and go to Connected devices > Android Auto > Customize launcher and ensure the MapQuest checkbox is actually checked.
Once these steps are complete — including joining the beta program — you should find MapQuest available to you in your vehicle.
Using MapQuest on Android Auto
Initial user feedback on MapQuest's Android Auto beta suggests the application remains a little rough around the edges in comparison to Google or Apple Maps. Various reports claim there have been complaints of app crashes, delayed response times and voice navigation prompts that cut off in the middle of sentences. Interface quirks have been identified, and there may be some frustration that some real-time features are limited to North America (US and Canada).
To be fair, this is beta software; flaws and foibles are to be expected, and the company's social media feeds suggest its developers are actively working to improve the app, including regular software patches.
What features does MapQuest on Android Auto provide?
MapQuest's Android Auto solution currently provides:
- Turn-by-turn navigation
- Real-time traffic updates
- Route optimization
- Search for locations, such as gas stations or EV chargers
- Favorites and saved locations
- Voice search
- Speedometer display to show current speed against the speed limit
- Crowdsourced incident reporting
While the software moves through the beta process, drivers seeking immediate alternatives for Android Auto or Apple's CarPlay may also want to try and download Waze, Sygic or TomTom Go.

excerpt_fa: Apple is collaborating with LG on a new lineup of smart home devices, including a video doorbell, thermostat, indoor camera, and more, according to a report from Bloomberg. The products will reportedly feature LG branding but integrate with the company's rumored smart home hub...
content_en:
Apple is collaborating with LG on a new lineup of smart home devices, including a video doorbell, thermostat, indoor camera, and more, according to a report from Bloomberg. The products will reportedly feature LG branding but integrate with the company’s rumored smart home hub that’s expected to launch during an event on October 13th.
Apple and LG team up on new smart home gear, starting with a lock, doorbell, and thermostat
Bloomberg reports that newly-surfaced LG smart home gear is part of a ‘second-party’ development arrangement with Apple.
Bloomberg reports that newly-surfaced LG smart home gear is part of a ‘second-party’ development arrangement with Apple.
Sources tell Bloomberg that the upcoming line of devices also includes a deadbolt lock, outdoor security camera, and a floodlight camera.
Several of the devices will reportedly come with support for the smart home protocols Thread and Matter amid a “formal reboot” for Apple’s HomeKit platform. The door lock also comes with an ultra-wideband feature that could allow it to automatically unlock when a user gets near their door, according to Bloomberg.
For months, rumors have suggested that Apple is planning to dive deeper into the smart home space. The company is working on a Siri AI-enabled smart home hub that comes with a six-inch display that users can mount to their wall or place on a table, Bloomberg has reported. Apple is expected to take the wraps off the upcoming device later this month, where it may also reveal a new HomePod mini and an upgraded Apple TV device.

title_en: Sebastian Maniscalco’s SiriusXM channel is hurting up-and-coming talent, comics say
title_fa: Sebastian Maniscalco’s SiriusXM channel is hurting up-and-coming talent, comics say
excerpt_en: Comedian Sebastian Maniscalco is facing backlash from fellow comics who claim his takeover of SiriusXM's Raw Comedy channel is harming up-and-coming talent, as reported earlier by Deadline. Many established comics, including Patton Oswalt and Margaret Cho, have posted videos...
excerpt_fa: Comedian Sebastian Maniscalco is facing backlash from fellow comics who claim his takeover of SiriusXM's Raw Comedy channel is harming up-and-coming talent, as reported earlier by Deadline. Many established comics, including Patton Oswalt and Margaret Cho, have posted videos...
content_en:
Comedian Sebastian Maniscalco is facing backlash from fellow comics who claim his takeover of SiriusXM’s Raw Comedy channel is harming up-and-coming talent, as reported earlier by Deadline. Many established comics, including Patton Oswalt and Margaret Cho, have posted videos online calling on Maniscalco to carry on Raw Comedy’s legacy by highlighting newer comedians on his channel, instead of mostly focusing on well-known ones.
Sebastian Maniscalco’s SiriusXM channel is hurting up-and-coming talent, comics say
Maniscalco’s channel replaced SiriusXM’s Raw Comedy, which highlighted a wider pool of more than 800 comics.
Maniscalco’s channel replaced SiriusXM’s Raw Comedy, which highlighted a wider pool of more than 800 comics.
SiriusXM launched Sebastian Maniscalco’s Comedy Radio in April, which is “curated and headlined by Sebastian himself,” according to the satellite radio provider. The move replaced SiriusXM’s long-running Raw Comedy channel featuring uncensored stand-up comedy shows from a range of talent. Now, the channel airs Maniscalco’s own show, alongside a stream of stand-up content that comedian Dan Soder says features “very famous comics who are dead or who don’t necessarily need the money.”
The widespread criticism comes as Stand Up for Standup, a nonprofit organization that provides resources for comedians in need, published a report about the channel’s shift away from emerging talent, who rely not only on the visibility they receive from appearing on the station, but also on the royalties they earn from SiriusXM. The organization says that since March, the spins on Maniscalco’s channels have decreased from a wider net of more than 800 comics to a much narrower pool of 275 artists, largely skewed toward celebrities.
“We believe this shift, both in the overall quantity of artists enjoying plays on Channel 102, and the change in distribution across all spin-getters favoring the top few, is bad for comedians, and bad for the future of comedy,” Stand Up for Standup says.
“There’s a lot of up-and-coming comedians who are depending on the money and the checks that they get from Sirius,” Oswalt says in an Instagram video. “But 500 of them have been booted off of Sirius… You can easily reverse this decision. Get those young comedians back on the Sirius channel. Let them get those checks.” Many other comedians, including Liz Miele, Kyle Kinane, and Michelle Wolf, have called out Maniscalco as well.
In a statement to Deadline, SiriusXM says Maniscalco’s channel “introduced a new creative direction and a regularly evolving programming mix for the channel,” adding that “SiriusXM continues to invest in comedians more than any other audio platform.” Neither SiriusXM nor representatives for Maniscalco immediately responded to The Verge’s request for comment.

Now, the channel airs Maniscalco’s own show, alongside a stream of stand-up content that comedian Dan Soder says features “very famous comics who are dead or who don’t necessarily need the money.”
The widespread criticism comes as Stand Up for Standup, a nonprofit organization that provides resources for comedians in need, published a report about the channel’s shift away from emerging talent, who rely not only on the visibility they receive from appearing on the station, but also on the royalties they earn from SiriusXM. The organization says that since March, the spins on Maniscalco’s channels have decreased from a wider net of more than 800 comics to a much narrower pool of 275 artists, largely skewed toward celebrities.
“We believe this shift, both in the overall quantity of artists enjoying plays on Channel 102, and the change in distribution across all spin-getters favoring the top few, is bad for comedians, and bad for the future of comedy,” Stand Up for Standup says.
“There’s a lot of up-and-coming comedians who are depending on the money and the checks that they get from Sirius,” Oswalt says in an Instagram video. “But 500 of them have been booted off of Sirius… You can easily reverse this decision. Get those young comedians back on the Sirius channel. Let them get those checks.” Many other comedians, including Liz Miele, Kyle Kinane, and Michelle Wolf, have called out Maniscalco as well.
In a statement to Deadline, SiriusXM says Maniscalco’s channel “introduced a new creative direction and a regularly evolving programming mix for the channel,” adding that “SiriusXM continues to invest in comedians more than any other audio platform.” Neither SiriusXM nor representatives for Maniscalco immediately responded to The Verge’s request for comment.

title_en: Silicon Valley’s AI wunderkind launches Underdog, the most private Instinct/Muse competitor yet
title_fa: Silicon Valley’s AI wunderkind launches Underdog, the most private Instinct/Muse competitor yet
excerpt_en: Sigil Wen, backed by a Silicon Valley who's who, has built an on-device AI assistant that promises to be free, fully private, and capable for everyday tasks.
excerpt_fa: Sigil Wen, backed by a Silicon Valley who's who, has built an on-device AI assistant that promises to be free, fully private, and capable for everyday tasks.
content_en:
When self-taught coder Sigil Wen was 17, he moved to Silicon Valley and lived in an AI hacker house with famed AI researcher Andrej Karpathy.
While there, he hacked and coded alongside other people who would become the biggest names in AI, like Perplexity founder Aravind Srinivas and OpenAI researcher Noam Brown. He tested early versions of AI tools that would later become well known, including a chatbot shared by Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann that would become Claude, an image generator from David Holz that would become Midjourney, and what would become OpenAI’s GPT-3 and the image generator Stable Diffusion. Prominent investor and entrepreneur Naval Ravikant hired him for Airchat, Ravikant’s now-defunct rival to the Clubhouse social network.
For fun, he figured out how to get GPT-2 running on his Apple Watch. “It was a magical time,” Wen told TechCrunch.
Now a Thiel Fellow — the program from investor Peter Thiel that invites young founders to pursue projects instead of college — Wen on Monday launched an invite-only beta of Underdog, one of the most private AI assistants Silicon Valley has yet to offer. The model runs wholly on-device, meaning the user’s data remains on devices they already own, currently Macs and Windows PCs, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions coming soon.
Underdog is powered by Husky, the inference engine Wen built to run AI models quickly on a user’s own hardware. Wen says it moves less data between a computer’s main chip and its graphics chip than rival on-device engines.
Underdog has other security features baked in, too, like encrypting the keys to the email and other accounts that users authorize Underdog to access.
Underdog is, however, using much smaller models than today’s state-of-the-art ones hosted in data centers. It currently uses a 27-billion parameter reasoning model fine-tuned from Qwen3.8-27B.
Wen argues that this model compares favorably with Claude Opus 4.6 in some benchmarks, or what was considered top performance six months ago. He says that means it can handle the everyday tasks that people want an AI assistant to do, like shopping research or answering math homework questions.
“You don’t need to sacrifice your privacy for the capability because they’re just as capable,” Wen says. He adds that small on-device models will continue to grow more capable over time.
Perhaps the most interesting thing about Underdog is its early business model. The app will be free at first and never ad-supported. Since the AI runs on users’ machines, Underdog doesn’t have the giant overhead of paying a provider for inference. “I don’t have to charge you a subscription to run this because my costs are so super low,” he said.
Instead, with Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison as one of his angel investors, he’s borrowing a play from the fintech era. Underdog will take a tiny percentage of payment transactions that the AI assistant makes using Stripe’s secure payment rails, something like an interchange fee. In this way, the AI assistant never has to mine your data. It is as aligned with you as your bank or credit card providers.
This runs contrary to the business motivations of many of the other players in AI assistants, whose privacy policies allow them to collect data on users that they may sell to advertisers or other third parties, or use to train other models.
That kind of data collection could be a particularly treacherous trade-off for users of an AI assistant, which may need access to the most intimate details about you in order to be useful, from medical conditions to financial data to data on your kids.
As Wen wrote in what he calls his AI manifesto, “Why should using AI require surrendering your private information?”
He tells TechCrunch: “I honestly want to build Underdog for myself. I’m building a product that I would be proud for my future children to use.”
The startup behind Underdog is named Conway Research, and Collison isn’t its only big-name investor. Conway is backed by Andreessen Horowitz via partner Chris Dixon, as well as Khosla Ventures, Hummingbird, SV Angel, the Anthology Fund (the partnership fund between Menlo Ventures and Anthropic), and a prominent list of angel investors that includes Vercel founder Guillermo Rauch, Noam Brown, and Deedy Das, among others.

title_en: Tesla’s Model 3 and Model Y can be a backup battery for your house
title_fa: Tesla’s Model 3 and Model Y can be a backup battery for your house
excerpt_en: Some Tesla Model 3 and Model Y owners can use their EV battery to keep the lights on longer during a power outage, now that Tesla's expanding the Powershare Home Backup feature. It was previously only available on the Cybertruck, and also requires owning Tesla's Powerwall 3....
excerpt_fa: Some Tesla Model 3 and Model Y owners can use their EV battery to keep the lights on longer during a power outage, now that Tesla's expanding the Powershare Home Backup feature. It was previously only available on the Cybertruck, and also requires owning Tesla's Powerwall 3....
content_en:
Some Tesla Model 3 and Model Y owners can use their EV battery to keep the lights on longer during a power outage, now that Tesla’s expanding the Powershare Home Backup feature. It was previously only available on the Cybertruck, and also requires owning Tesla’s Powerwall 3. However, support for the Powerwall 2 and Powerwall Plus is “coming soon.” Tesla’s EVs aren’t the first or only ones with bidirectional charging; companies like Kia and GM also offer vehicle-to-home power on their vehicles, while Nissan’s Leaf offered power-to-grid charging years ago.
Tesla’s Model 3 and Model Y can be a backup battery for your house
You can get up to a couple of days of power with the Model 3 or Model Y if you also have Tesla’s Powerwall 3.
You can get up to a couple of days of power with the Model 3 or Model Y if you also have Tesla’s Powerwall 3.
Tesla says the Model 3 and Model Y can extend home backup power to over two days for Premium and Performance models, which is shorter than the “over three days” Tesla claims you can get from the Cybertruck’s battery.
As Electrek points out, Tesla is only guaranteeing Home Backup will work on Model 3 and Model Y vehicles ordered from October 1st onward because not all older models include the PCS2 Lite inverter required to make it all work. So far, the feature is also only mentioned as available in the US and Puerto Rico, but not Canada, and not for the larger Model S or Model X. Tesla’s Powershare Grid Support feature is also still exclusive to the Cybertruck.

title_en: How AI decision models could change content moderation
title_fa: How AI decision models could change content moderation
excerpt_en: On Tuesday, Musubi announced a lightweight decision model made for real-time moderation called PolicyLM-1.7B, released with open weights.
excerpt_fa: On Tuesday, Musubi announced a lightweight decision model made for real-time moderation called PolicyLM-1.7B, released with open weights.
content_en:
As decision models spread across the industry, a company called Musubi has a new idea for how to put them to work: moderating content. On Tuesday, Musubi announced a lightweight decision model made for real-time moderation called PolicyLM-1.7B, released with open weights.
The idea is to take a content policy written in plain English and apply it to messages in under 50 milliseconds. Musubi’s model is designed to be similar in cost and speed to the AI classifier systems that power moderation on most social platforms — but because it has the flexibility of a modern LLM, it can apply complex policies without special training. Even more important, the model won’t need new training when the policy changes, allowing for human policy-setters to iterate as much as they need.
As Musubi co-founder and chief AI officer Filip Jankovic sees it, it gives platform managers a way to label content proactively.
“Product teams just want a better understanding of what’s happening on their platform, especially as the amount of content is exponentially increasing,” Jankovic says. “Being able to label all of that in a very scalable, customizable way is extremely useful.”
Decision models have become a hot topic in the AI world since the release of TypeSafe AI’s Jev in September, which was shortly followed by competing decision models from OpenAI and Amazon. Instead of outputting text, a decision model outputs outcome probabilities, though in this case the model outputs a binary judgement: Either the content is in the category or it isn’t. By limiting the model’s output to a set of predetermined choices, decision models are able to run faster and cheaper than large language models, while still maintaining the flexibility of the transformer architecture.
One early use case is reining in misbehavior by AI agents — so it’s only natural to apply the same technology to human misbehavior.
Notably, Jankovic says his interest in decision models predates Jev, tracing it back to a 2024 project called GLiNER (Generalist Model for Named Entity Recognition) that deployed many of the same techniques.
Still, Musubi isn’t wary of the comparison. If anything, the company is eager to use the new interest in decision models to shine a light on content moderation. “If Jev caught your eye, PolicyLM-1.7B is the same kind of model, trained specifically for content moderation, that you can run yourself,” the product announcement reads.

title_en: Google’s power-hungry data centers crave nuclear energy
title_fa: Google’s power-hungry data centers crave nuclear energy
excerpt_en: Google announced a new agreement to update six nuclear power plant sites across the US as the tech giant seeks to generate more electricity for its power-hungry data centers. Google signed the 20-year deal with Constellation, the leading nuclear power plant operator in the US....
excerpt_fa: Google announced a new agreement to update six nuclear power plant sites across the US as the tech giant seeks to generate more electricity for its power-hungry data centers. Google signed the 20-year deal with Constellation, the leading nuclear power plant operator in the US....
content_en:
Google announced a new agreement to update six nuclear power plant sites across the US as the tech giant seeks to generate more electricity for its power-hungry data centers.
Google’s power-hungry data centers crave nuclear energy
Google signed long-term agreements meant to cover the costs of upgrades at nuclear power plants.
Google signed long-term agreements meant to cover the costs of upgrades at nuclear power plants.
Google signed the 20-year deal with Constellation, the leading nuclear power plant operator in the US. The power purchase agreement is meant to guarantee the revenue needed to cover the cost of efficiency upgrades at existing nuclear plants and “represents more than $4.3 billion of new investment by Constellation,” according to the press release.
Over the next five years, the companies expect new equipment at each site to collectively lead to 890 megawatts of additional nuclear capacity. That’s roughly equivalent to the amount of electricity one large new nuclear reactor or three small modular reactors might generate, according to Google and Constellation.
PJM has struggled lately to meet growing demand from AI data centers
They plan to modernize 11 reactors at six sites in Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. Each is connected to the PJM Interconnection grid, the largest power grid in the US, which spans 13 states and the District of Columbia — including the nation’s largest hub for data centers in Loudoun County, Virginia.
PJM has struggled lately to meet growing demand from AI data centers. An independent market monitor filed a complaint last year with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) saying that PJM was planning to allow huge data centers to connect to the grid that it could not reliably serve, which could lead to blackouts.
In January, the Trump administration and governors from all of the states where PJM operates issued a joint statement calling on PJM to hold an “emergency” power auction to support the buildout of new power plants through long-term contracts. PJM postponed its auction last week following a directive from FERC to revise its proposal in order to ensure stronger protections to prevent data centers from raising electricity bills for other customers. Electricity rates have skyrocketed in states connected to PJM, including New Jersey, where prices have climbed 54 percent over five years.
Along with the nuclear power deal, Google also inked a separate, much larger 15-year energy supply agreement with Constellation meant to guarantee continued revenue for other existing power plants Constellation operates within PJM, regardless of fuel type. Nuclear energy made up 70 percent of Constellation’s total generating capacity last year, and another 8 percent came from renewables. Gas and oil made up the remaining 22 percent, according to the company’s latest sustainability report. Gas also accounts for the largest chunk of PJM’s fuel mix. At 2,700MW, the second deal is much larger than the nuclear power purchase agreement.
Data centers are driving a surge in new gas infrastructure projects in the US, moving many tech companies further from their sustainability goals. Google’s carbon emissions rose by 18 percent last year along with a jump in electricity demand of 37 percent, according to the company’s latest sustainability report.

title_en: AI computing startup Lambda to raise $4B ahead of planned IPO
title_fa: AI computing startup Lambda to raise $4B ahead of planned IPO
excerpt_en: Nvidia-backed Lambda is raising up to $4 billion at a $14.5 billion pre-money valuation ahead of a planned 2027 IPO, led by Coatue and Blackstone.
excerpt_fa: Nvidia-backed Lambda is raising up to $4 billion at a $14.5 billion pre-money valuation ahead of a planned 2027 IPO, led by Coatue and Blackstone.
content_en:
Cloud provider Lambda is raising up to $4 billion at a $14.5 billion pre-money valuation, marking what could be its last private round before a planned 2027 IPO, according to The Wall Street Journal. Coatue Management and Blackstone are leading the round.
A letter to investors reviewed by the Journal shows Lambda’s backlog grew from $15 billion in June to $50 billion in September. While that might look like a hearty increase in demand, much of that increase appears to be driven by a $35 billion commitment from one company: Anthropic, which signed a deal with Lambda in late August.
That means Lambda’s valuation, which has climbed significantly since its 2025 funding round, could be leaning heavily on Anthropic’s ability to keep paying. Still, with reliable GPU capacity so scarce, investors are clearly still willing to bet on companies that provide it, especially ones with large contracts with a major AI lab.
For neoclouds like Lambda, demand isn’t so much the problem as is the cost of meeting it. Data center buildouts are largely funded by debt — of which Lambda just raised an additional $1 billion last week — and lenders are getting choosier about who they offer cash to and under what circumstances. Lambda’s decision to raise more now not only sets the tone for its IPO pricing, but also gives it access to more capital before the scrutiny of public markets arrives.
If and when Lambda does IPO — the company was reportedly meant to debut this year, but has pushed that back amid market uncertainty — it will join other Nvidia-backed neoclouds, like CoreWeave and Nebius, that now depend on the health of their stock to fund their data center buildouts. British neocloud Nscale filed for an IPO last month and is expected to begin trading soon.
Lambda, Coatue, and Blackstone did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title_fa: Amazon’s last-gen Kindle Paperwhite is 30 percent off
excerpt_en: Calling something “last-gen” usually means it comes with big compromises compared to the latest version. That’s not as true for the last-gen Kindle Paperwhite as it is with some other tech. The newer version can open books 30 percent faster (not the same as page-turning speed),...
excerpt_fa: Calling something “last-gen” usually means it comes with big compromises compared to the latest version. That’s not as true for the last-gen Kindle Paperwhite as it is with some other tech. The newer version can open books 30 percent faster (not the same as page-turning speed),...
content_en:
Calling something “last-gen” usually means it comes with big compromises compared to the latest version. That’s not as true for the last-gen Kindle Paperwhite as it is with some other tech. The newer version can open books 30 percent faster (not the same as page-turning speed), and its aluminum design is a millimeter thinner — but it costs $50 more.
Amazon’s last-gen Kindle Paperwhite is 30 percent off
$170 gets you the Signature Edition without ads, plus 32GB of storage and wireless charging.
$170 gets you the Signature Edition without ads, plus 32GB of storage and wireless charging.
The 2024 edition has the same fantastic 300ppi screen, an auto-adjusting front light, and waterproof (IPX8) design. And the Signature Edition that’s discounted has no lockscreen ads, twice the storage (32GB) of the base model, plus wireless charging and an ambient light sensor, and it’s down to $169.99 (originally $249.99) at Amazon.
Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition
The premium Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition offers the same design and performance as the standard model but with more storage and support for wireless charging.
The standard Paperwhite is $149.99 (was $199.99) at Amazon, and while the lower price is nice, I’d suggest only opting for that model if you’re alright with what you’re giving up (which is a lot): it has half the storage, no wireless charging, and lockscreen ads.
