title_en: What are the benefits of having a second monitor?
title_fa: What are the benefits of having a second monitor?
excerpt_en: Adding a second monitor is a huge upgrade, even if you aren't doing intensive work like editing video or accounting. More screen space is always helpful.
excerpt_fa: Adding a second monitor is a huge upgrade, even if you aren't doing intensive work like editing video or accounting. More screen space is always helpful.
content_en:
What are the benefits of having a second monitor?
Two screens means more real estate to run apps without having to switch between them all the time.
Upgrading to dual monitors is the best workflow upgrade you can make, with some studies indicating that it can boost productivity and satisfaction. Whether it's for multitasking, to expand a split-screen view, gaming or everyday office tasks, there's a lot of value in this setup.
While you might think dual screens are mostly for gamers or those who work in computer-intensive fields like music and video production or accounting, that's not the case. My best friend works in insurance and uses a dual-monitor setup so she can copy and paste information from one document to another instead of switching tabs, or put her Teams chat on one monitor while working on the other. She added that "Dragging and dropping documents is so easy." Bottom line: there are plenty of benefits for anyone who regularly multitasks.
Usability advantages of a second monitor
The most obvious reason to set up two of the best monitors is being able to spread your work across multiple screens. The app I use most on my MacBook is split-screen, so I can write on one half while conducting web research or going through PDF briefs on the other. The benefit of having two full-sized monitors to do this, versus half a screen with small font, is easy to realize. Creative professionals or data analysts, meanwhile, can expand the screen real estate and see more at once. Professions like traders and programmers may benefit from three or even four monitors. But for most people, two is the sweet spot.
It's worthwhile for any kind of multitasking. I always have tons of tabs open on my computer and consistently use two separate web browsers. You can work on two tasks at the same time, like tweaking your resume on one monitor while hunting through job listings on the other. A second monitor can be home for communication apps or other mostly-static information you want to keep an eye on, like your email inbox.
Beyond text-based documents like word processing and spreadsheets, two monitors are great for gamers. You can play on one screen and use the second to manage game recording, chat with your streaming audience, access Discord and more without having to leave the game. During a video call, you can take notes on one display while looking at your team on the other. Or if you're making a how-to video, you could have a script open on one monitor while you perform the steps on the second.
Dual monitor organization and tips
Having a second monitor allows for better organization, both on your desk and the screens. I sometimes print reference documents to view them separately. A second monitor would eliminate the need to do this, saving paper (and clutter). By not relying on a phone or tablet as a second screen, you avoid the risk of getting caught up in mobile distractions.
It's worth noting that you don't necessarily need a high-end second monitor. Specs like high refresh rate are more important for the display you're looking at most of the time. For a second one you use only when necessary, a more affordable monitor is fine. Ideally, you should find a second monitor that is the same size as your first for a seamless look. It should also have the same pixel density to ensure matching text and image scaling. Finally, get mounting hardware to situate them at the same level.
Be aware of how far you should sit from your monitor, as well as the proper eye height, and set them up accordingly. You'll need to find a tidy way to connect both monitors to your computer, which requires two video outputs and the appropriate cables. Then, adjust display settings like brightness and contrast as needed.
If you're using a laptop, you might need to configure it to stay running when you close the lid if you aren't using it as one of your displays. Most modern MacBooks can support at least two monitors, for instance.
A second monitor might not be something you use all the time. But having it there when you need it can be, as my friend noted, a "complete game-changer." Being able to look at one program while working in another one saves you from constantly switching app windows and lets you keep an eye on what's most important.

title_en: How did retro consoles handle graphics before modern GPUs?
title_fa: How did retro consoles handle graphics before modern GPUs?
excerpt_en: Graphics chips could draw but not compute, until the Xbox arrived.
excerpt_fa: Graphics chips could draw but not compute, until the Xbox arrived.
content_en:
How did retro consoles handle graphics before modern GPUs?
Graphics chips could draw but not compute, until the Xbox arrived.
Console graphics came from bespoke, fixed-function chips for more than two decades, until the original Xbox burst onto the scene in 2001 with a PC GPU inside. Those of us who played on early consoles like the NES will have come across some familiar quirks with those fixed-function chips: When too many Goombas lined up on the same row in Super Mario Bros., for example, some of them would start to flicker. That's the NES's graphics chip hitting its hard limit of eight sprites per scanline; the chip drops anything past eight, and the game alternates which ones.
In the NES, it was the Ricoh 2C02 Picture Processing Unit that rendered game graphics. A pretty rudimentary chip, it couldn't run any code. Instead, it took tile artwork from the cartridge and a couple of lookup tables from memory and turned them into a TV signal, one scanline at a time. That arrangement — a dedicated picture generator fed by the CPU — is how most consoles rendered their graphics from the late 1970s into the 2000s.
When Microsoft's first Xbox came out in November 2001, it didn't look much like any console before it. Instead, it was built around an Intel Pentium III and a graphics chip NVIDIA made specially for it, based on the GeForce 3. The GeForce 3 had only been announced that February, and it was the first GPU that let developers program their own pixel and vertex shaders.
Sprites and scanlines
The NES' Ricoh 2C02 worked from about 10kB of memory. That's broken down into roughly 8kB of tile shapes stored on the cartridge and 2kB of RAM in the console holding a background map or two. Separate small memories inside the chip tracked things like the position, shape and orientation of up to 64 sprites. Its output was 256x240 pixels, built from 8x8 tiles.
As the CRT TV's electron beam swept across each line of the screen, the 2C02 worked out which 8x8 tile belonged at each spot. It then cross-referenced this with which sprites were sat on that line and decided which pixel to show. This took place in step with the beam, so the CPU couldn't safely rewrite the picture while it was being drawn.
Unlike the NES, the earlier Atari 2600 made the CPU also handle graphics. Because its Television Interface Adaptor had no frame buffer, the processor had to feed new values to the chip for every scanline drawn by the beam. Just five years earlier in 1972, the Magnavox Odyssey had no processor or memory, period, drawing its dots and lines with discrete diode-transistor logic. All of these machines were designed around a CRT, which is partly why retro games look better on old CRT TVs.
The PlayStation 2's custom silicon shared the load
Sony showed off the PS2's chips in March 1999. The CPU was the Emotion Engine, a 128-bit design Sony built with Toshiba, and graphics went to a separate chip called the Graphics Synthesizer. In the final consoles, the two ran at about 295 MHz and 147 MHz.
The Graphics Synthesizer didn't do any geometry work, though. By the time a triangle reached it, it had already been placed within the frame, and all the chip had to do was fill it in with color and texture. The geometry work happened back on the Emotion Engine, in two vector units. The CPU could give VU0 odd jobs, while VU1 mostly ran the 3D transforms that turned a game's models into on-screen triangles. Sony and Toshiba's engineers said a single vector unit could manage 85 million of those transforms a second. While no two consoles were the same, many early 3D consoles similarly shared the graphical load across multiple chips.
Interestingly, Sony had used the term GPU for the 1994 PlayStation's Toshiba-designed graphics chip. That's five years before NVIDIA marketed the GeForce 256 as the world's first GPU. But the working definition of a modern GPU, a chip that runs small programs written by the game, only came with GeForce 3 in early 2001.
The original Xbox and everything after
NVIDIA and Microsoft signed their Xbox deal in March 2000, and five days later, Bill Gates took to the stage and announced the console. It would use an Intel Pentium III-class processor, a custom NVIDIA graphics processor, 64MB of memory shared by both and an 8GB hard drive. The finished box was unveiled at CES 2001 and then went on sale that November.
But consoles didn't make the switch to PC-style hardware all at once. The Nintendo GameCube launched the same month with a PowerPC processor from IBM, and every major console used one for the next decade: the Xbox 360 dropped Intel for three PowerPC cores from IBM in 2005, the PS3's Cell chip was built by Sony, Toshiba and IBM around a PowerPC core and the Wii and Wii U both ran updated versions of the GameCube's IBM chip.
The graphics side had already gone PC-style, with the 360's ATI chip and the PS3's NVIDIA one, but the processors hadn't. That changed in 2013, when the PS4 moved to eight AMD processor cores and a graphics design taken from AMD's Radeon PC cards. Today's PS5 and Xbox Series X each run eight AMD Zen 2 cores alongside AMD RDNA 2 graphics on the same chip as the CPU. Ultimately, designing graphics chips from scratch for consoles stopped making sense once off-the-shelf GPU architectures fit a console's budget.

title_en: The reason the Mac mini is cheaper than a MacBook
title_fa: The reason the Mac mini is cheaper than a MacBook
excerpt_en: If you're trying to decide between a MacBook and a Mac mini, you might be interested to know why there's a price difference.
excerpt_fa: If you're trying to decide between a MacBook and a Mac mini, you might be interested to know why there's a price difference.
content_en:
The reason the Mac mini is cheaper than a MacBook
If you're looking at base configurations, anyway.
For a while, the Mac mini was ranked as one of the best deals in computing. Arguably, it's still pretty great. For $900, you can get a Mac with Apple's new M6 processor, which is vastly overpowered for most of the apps the average person runs. You might max it out if you're running something like DaVinci Resolve or Resident Evil, but you're never going to touch its potential with an app like Safari or VLC. The only real weak point is that the base mini ships with just 256GB of storage, which can run out quickly if you sync your personal photo and video collections.
Strictly speaking, you can get a cheaper MacBook in the form of the Neo, but that introduces serious compromises, like 8GB of RAM and the same A18 Pro processor found in the iPhone 16 Pro. The next step up, the MacBook Air, is $1,100, and you're still stuck with an M5 chip and 16GB of RAM. A MacBook Pro might as well be in the stratosphere if you're searching for an affordable computer.
The dichotomy between mini and MacBook prices is pretty straightforward in most respects, owing to what's included versus what's not. But there are also deeper engineering elements at play. In the end, a MacBook Air might still be the most affordable option if you're planning to leap the hedges into Apple's walled garden.
How is a Mac mini more affordable than a MacBook Air?
The most obvious cost factor is the absence of a display. Though Apple never publishes an official bill of materials for its products, a replacement MacBook display can cost several hundred dollars if you're not covered by AppleCare. The actual manufacturing cost is likely far lower — nevertheless, Apple not only has to pay for the panel, but also the frame, hinge and cabling it's anchored to. The mini ships without a display or an embedded Center Stage camera, not that it would make much sense to put a webcam on a computer you might shove in a cabinet.
Also, while the mini has more ports than the Neo or Air — eight versus three, excluding dedicated power — it doesn't ship with any input peripherals. There's no keyboard, and no mouse or trackpad. Those may be relatively cheap add-ons if you don't have existing ones, yet it's another way Apple slashes manufacturing costs and lowers the sticker price, if not necessarily the practical amount you have to spend.
Another separator is the lack of a battery. This probably doesn't cut costs as much as ditching a display, since Apple charges anywhere between $150 and $250 for MacBook battery service, and that includes labor. Lithium-ion packs still aren't cheap, though, as anyone who's bought an EV or PEV will tell you. All the mini requires is an AC power supply.
Lastly, there are fundamental engineering differences between laptop and desktop computers. Although the mini does rely on some laptop-style components to achieve its form factor, it doesn't need to be thin, drop-resistant or maximally power-efficient. Its cooling system revolves around a giant circular vent at the base — something you could never get away with on a MacBook. Mobility and miniaturization are inherently expensive, which is part of how Apple can charge $700 for a Neo when the iPhone 16 Pro originally sold for $1,000.
Does it make more sense to buy a MacBook or a Mac mini?
If you're new to the Mac ecosystem and don't care about having a large screen, a MacBook Air is almost always the better value. Yes, $1,300 is a big ask, and Apple has yet to upgrade it to the M6 chip as of this writing. But you're getting a display, keyboard and trackpad out of the box, whereas you could easily spend more than that on peripherals for a Mac mini. You likely don't need the M6's performance, and going with a MacBook gives you the ability to operate from anywhere.
Where the mini shines through is for people who want to work from their TV or already have a monitor and other desktop peripherals. In those situations, there's no sense paying for a MacBook's additions unless you want the freedom to transition between home and mobile use. A mini actually has a distinct advantage in a desktop context, namely its two USB-C and three Thunderbolt ports. On a MacBook, possibly even a Pro, you might need to buy a dock to connect all your accessories.
Something we haven't touched on yet is the mini's upgradability. You can't swap parts in and out like a Windows PC, unfortunately, but if you need an industrial workhorse, the mini has more initial configuration options. A top-of-the-line mini would actually cost $6,800. That nets you an M5 Pro, 64GB of RAM, 8TB of storage and 10 Gbps Ethernet. It's that storage that's the killer. Dropping back to 512GB brings prices down to $3,000, though at that point, you might get more value out of a Mac Studio, which starts with an M5 Max chip and 36GB of RAM for just $2,500.

The reason the Mac mini is cheaper than a MacBook
If you're looking at base configurations, anyway.
For a while, the Mac mini was ranked as one of the best deals in computing. Arguably, it's still pretty great. For $900, you can get a Mac with Apple's new M6 processor, which is vastly overpowered for most of the apps the average person runs. You might max it out if you're running something like DaVinci Resolve or Resident Evil, but you're never going to touch its potential with an app like Safari or VLC. The only real weak point is that the base mini ships with just 256GB of storage, which can run out quickly if you sync your personal photo and video collections.
Strictly speaking, you can get a cheaper MacBook in the form of the Neo, but that introduces serious compromises, like 8GB of RAM and the same A18 Pro processor found in the iPhone 16 Pro. The next step up, the MacBook Air, is $1,100, and you're still stuck with an M5 chip and 16GB of RAM. A MacBook Pro might as well be in the stratosphere if you're searching for an affordable computer.
The dichotomy between mini and MacBook prices is pretty straightforward in most respects, owing to what's included versus what's not. But there are also deeper engineering elements at play. In the end, a MacBook Air might still be the most affordable option if you're planning to leap the hedges into Apple's walled garden.
How is a Mac mini more affordable than a MacBook Air?
The most obvious cost factor is the absence of a display. Though Apple never publishes an official bill of materials for its products, a replacement MacBook display can cost several hundred dollars if you're not covered by AppleCare. The actual manufacturing cost is likely far lower — nevertheless, Apple not only has to pay for the panel, but also the frame, hinge and cabling it's anchored to. The mini ships without a display or an embedded Center Stage camera, not that it would make much sense to put a webcam on a computer you might shove in a cabinet.
Also, while the mini has more ports than the Neo or Air — eight versus three, excluding dedicated power — it doesn't ship with any input peripherals. There's no keyboard, and no mouse or trackpad. Those may be relatively cheap add-ons if you don't have existing ones, yet it's another way Apple slashes manufacturing costs and lowers the sticker price, if not necessarily the practical amount you have to spend.
Another separator is the lack of a battery. This probably doesn't cut costs as much as ditching a display, since Apple charges anywhere between $150 and $250 for MacBook battery service, and that includes labor. Lithium-ion packs still aren't cheap, though, as anyone who's bought an EV or PEV will tell you. All the mini requires is an AC power supply.
Lastly, there are fundamental engineering differences between laptop and desktop computers. Although the mini does rely on some laptop-style components to achieve its form factor, it doesn't need to be thin, drop-resistant or maximally power-efficient. Its cooling system revolves around a giant circular vent at the base — something you could never get away with on a MacBook. Mobility and miniaturization are inherently expensive, which is part of how Apple can charge $700 for a Neo when the iPhone 16 Pro originally sold for $1,000.
Does it make more sense to buy a MacBook or a Mac mini?
If you're new to the Mac ecosystem and don't care about having a large screen, a MacBook Air is almost always the better value. Yes, $1,300 is a big ask, and Apple has yet to upgrade it to the M6 chip as of this writing. But you're getting a display, keyboard and trackpad out of the box, whereas you could easily spend more than that on peripherals for a Mac mini. You likely don't need the M6's performance, and going with a MacBook gives you the ability to operate from anywhere.
Where the mini shines through is for people who want to work from their TV or already have a monitor and other desktop peripherals. In those situations, there's no sense paying for a MacBook's additions unless you want the freedom to transition between home and mobile use. A mini actually has a distinct advantage in a desktop context, namely its two USB-C and three Thunderbolt ports. On a MacBook, possibly even a Pro, you might need to buy a dock to connect all your accessories.
Something we haven't touched on yet is the mini's upgradability. You can't swap parts in and out like a Windows PC, unfortunately, but if you need an industrial workhorse, the mini has more initial configuration options. A top-of-the-line mini would actually cost $6,800. That nets you an M5 Pro, 64GB of RAM, 8TB of storage and 10 Gbps Ethernet. It's that storage that's the killer. Dropping back to 512GB brings prices down to $3,000, though at that point, you might get more value out of a Mac Studio, which starts with an M5 Max chip and 36GB of RAM for just $2,500.

title_en: You should avoid using a screen protector on your MacBook — here's why
title_fa: You should avoid using a screen protector on your MacBook — here's why
excerpt_en: Screen protectors can do more harm than good.
excerpt_fa: Screen protectors can do more harm than good.
content_en:
You should avoid using a screen protector on your MacBook — here's why
Putting on a screen protector may have unintended consequences.
Putting a screen protector on expensive electronics is second nature for any experienced technology user, and in almost all cases is the smart choice for your device. Considering how much a new MacBook costs, it's a natural assumption that this same logic would apply. However, putting a screen protector on your MacBook can actually do more harm than good.
There are a lot of theoretical boons that come along with using a protector on your MacBook, especially if you're frequently transporting it from place to place. Fancier ones that boast privacy from prying eyes can be particularly appealing for anyone who frequently uses their laptop while out in public. A laptop is different from a phone, though, and in practice screen protectors really aren't that necessary — it's closed when on the move, and you aren't nearly as liable to drop it since it's used on a sturdy surface instead of one-handed. More so than that, though, the cons simply outweigh the benefits.
Why you shouldn't use a screen protector on a MacBook
From a purely aesthetic point of view, a screen protector on your MacBook can visibly dampen the display you spent good money on. A protector can scatter more light and reduce overall clarity, and with such a large surface area, the chances you're sticking one on with zero air bubbles is slim. However, the much bigger threat is to your screen's overall health, particularly the anti-reflective coating that sits on the top layer of the screen. It's something imperceptible so long as it's not damaged, but a screen protector can ruin it. When it comes time to replace your screen protector, peeling off of the adhesive can leave the coating cracked, peeling and frankly pretty ugly to look at.
Depending on the thickness and material of the screen protector, it can also stop your laptop from closing properly or cause damage to the screen even deeper than this top layer. A MacBook is designed to close with a very small gap between the screen and keyboard, and a thick glass screen protector can bridge that gap. If that's the case, the force of closing your laptop even a bit too hard could have a ripple effect from the base into the screen.
If you absolutely must get a screen protector for your MacBook, there are a few safe alternatives. There's the UltraThin Magnetic Privacy Screen Filter from Kensington, for example, which is sold on Apple's official website. Its magnetism prevents any of the dangers associated with adhesive, and its thinness eliminates the chance of force-based damage.
Other accessories can also be harmful
There are many useful MacBook accessories, but a screen protector isn't the only one that can be harmful to your computer. Many others that sound like safeguards can also be a detriment, like a hardshell case. A heavier hardshell case can wear out the MacBook's hinge, and depending on its design can also trap heat against your computer. To make sure your hardshell case is safe, make sure it's very lightweight and has vent cutouts. It's also important it doesn't stop your laptop from closing fully, as Apple warns any accessories that do so pose a risk of damaging your screen by disrupting the "tight tolerance" between screen and base.
In that same vein of preventing your laptop from closing properly, keyboard and webcam covers pose a similar risk. Over time, a keyboard cover can even leave permanent marks on your screen, since the microscopic gap between screen and keys no longer exists. A webcam cover can also potentially damage the screen due to disrupting the tight tolerance, as well as make a very useful feature, the ambient light sensor, no longer work. Apple recommends that if you must use a keyboard cover, remove it before closing your laptop, and if you need to use a webcam cover, make sure it's not thicker than an average sheet of printer paper.

title_en: Every Starlink Dish Available: How To Know Which Setup May Be Right For You
title_fa: Every Starlink Dish Available: How To Know Which Setup May Be Right For You
excerpt_en: Everyone has different needs when it comes to internet connectivity, and Starlink's dish selection caters to a many applications, from stationary to mobile.
excerpt_fa: Everyone has different needs when it comes to internet connectivity, and Starlink's dish selection caters to a many applications, from stationary to mobile.
content_en:
Every Starlink Dish Available: How To Know Which Setup May Be Right For You
From stationary to on-the-go connectivity needs.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
For years, getting Starlink meant buying whatever satellite dish the company was selling at the time, regardless of your needs. That's no longer the case. Starlink now offers multiple options designed for everything from connecting a rural home to keeping an RV, boat or remote worksite online.
Choosing a Starlink dish isn't exactly difficult, but it's important to understand that the cheapest option, while appealing, won't always be the best. Alternatively, the most expensive option can be overkill. Portability, durability, performance and whether you need internet at a fixed location or on the move can all affect which setup makes sense for you.
There are six Starlink dishes total that we'll cover here, some available in slightly different versions or bundles.
Starlink V4
For most people, the V4, which headlines the Standard 4 and 4 X kits, is probably the Starlink dish to start with. It's positioned for residential users and everyday online activities like streaming, video calls and online gaming. The rectangular design isn't new to Starlink. The company moved away from its original circular terminal years ago, when Starlink's rectangular satellite broadband dish was introduced as a smaller, lighter alternative.
The V4 is a rectangular terminal without a built-in motor, so it relies on software-assisted manual orientation instead. The dish measures about 23.4 by 15 inches, weighs 6.4 pounds and has a 110-degree field of view. The biggest difference between the Standard 4 and Standard 4 X kits isn't the dish itself, but the equipment included. The Standard 4 comes with Starlink's smaller Router Mini, while the Standard 4 X includes the newer, faster Router 3. The Standard 4 is also sold as a complete kit with a kickstand, power supply and the cables needed to get connected.
The V4 is more than likely enough for most fixed home internet setups unless you have a specific need for portability, extra durability or higher performance. It's built the things most people expect from a home internet connection without paying for hardware built for RVs, boats or commercial applications.
Starlink V5
The Starlink V5 is the company's newest residential dish, but it isn't a performance upgrade over the previous V4. Starlink just made the hardware considerably smaller, lighter and more power-efficient. Starlink's V5 home dish is smaller and more energy-efficient than the V4, measuring about 15.1 by 12 inches and weighing 2.4 pounds, compared with 6.4 pounds for the V4.
The smaller size also comes with lower power consumption. Starlink lists average power use at 35 to 50 watts for the V5, compared with 75 to 100 watts for the V4. The tradeoff is a slightly lower peak download speed. Starlink lists up to 375 Mbps for the V5, compared with 400+ Mbps for the V4.
The V5 is intended for fixed home internet, not for use while a vehicle is moving. It comes with a Router Mini, a kickstand, a pipe adapter mount and a 15-meter cable, and Starlink says it is currently available only in select areas as production ramps up.
For someone setting up Starlink at home, the V5 is essentially the newer, smaller residential option. Its lower power consumption and lighter hardware could make it easier to install and cheaper to operate, but its availability is still limited and it doesn't offer higher peak speeds than the larger V4.
Starlink Mini
If you want to take your internet connection with you, the Starlink Mini is the most obvious choice. Starlink describes it as a compact, portable kit designed to provide high-speed, low-latency internet on the go or at home.
The name is pretty fitting. The Mini measures 11.75 by 10.2 inches and weighs about 2.4 pounds, making it significantly smaller and lighter than Starlink's Standard dish. That portability has been a major part of Starlink's appeal for travelers, and Starlink users can take their terminal on the road with the Mini. Its built-in Wi-Fi router also means you don't have to carry a separate router with you.
The Mini uses considerably less power than some of Starlink's larger dishes, with average consumption of 20 to 40 watts. It can even be powered using a compatible USB-C power source with Starlink's optional USB-C to barrel jack cable, which could make it especially useful for camping, road trips and other off-grid setups. SpaceX first sold the Starlink Mini for $599, but it has since dropped to $199 when purchased directly from Starlink.
It isn't just for travelers. The Starlink Mini is now widely available and doesn't need a residential subscription, making it an option for people who want to use it at home as well as on the road. Starlink says it offers download speeds of up to 300 Mbps. Portability is still the primary reason to choose it. If you're mainly looking for a permanent home internet setup, the Standard dish may be the more practical option.
Starlink Performance (Gen 2)
You may know the Starlink Performance (Gen 2) by its former name, the Flat High Performance Kit. The company originally developed this hardware for mobility, so Starlink internet service for RVs works on moving vehicles thanks to the dish's wider field of view and enhanced GPS capabilities.
That makes it more useful for vehicles and boats than the Standard dish. Starlink says its wider field of view can see more of the sky than the Standard dish, which can help it stay connected to passing satellites when a vehicle is moving or a boat is rocking on the water.
The hardware is designed for permanent installation instead of a quick setup. It comes with a wedge mount that positions the dish at an 8-degree tilt to help with water runoff. Starlink lists a 140-degree field of view, peak throughput of up to 450 Mbps for downloads and 60 Mbps for uploads, and a survivable wind speed of more than 174 mph.

title_en: When is it worth getting a sound card for your PC?
title_fa: When is it worth getting a sound card for your PC?
excerpt_en: Whether or not adding a sound card makes sense really depends on how you're regularly using your PC.
excerpt_fa: Whether or not adding a sound card makes sense really depends on how you're regularly using your PC.
content_en:
When is it worth getting a sound card for your PC?
Most people don't need to buy a sound card, but certain use cases can benefit from adding one.
Many eons ago, in the '80s and '90s, a dedicated sound card was a must-have for any PC gamer or musician. Your machine's built-in hardware was limited to bleeps and bloops, or at best some convoluted tricks to fudge low-res samples. Just having music and effects that didn't grate on your ears was a major advancement. You'd no more consider skipping a sound card back then than you would a 3D graphics card today.
As you've probably noticed, though, dedicated sound cards seem to have dropped off the radar. They are still a thing, yet even the one-time king of PC audio, Creative, seems to have relegated them to a sideshow. That might seem odd, given that in some ways, sound matters more than ever. It's common for media to be mixed for spatial audio formats like Dolby Atmos, which position sound "objects" in 3D space. There's also a push for lossless audio in both movies and music. Either of those can place serious demands on pipelines, as home theater owners will attest.
Standing on the outside, then, you might be understandably confused. Does a sound card still meaningfully improve audio quality? Should you consider one when building or upgrading a PC rig? The quick answer is that most shoppers can safely skip one, although there are cases when a separate audio interface is mandatory.
Why you probably don't need a dedicated sound card for your PC
PC audio technology is no longer an afterthought, as it was in the '80s. It's taken for granted that anyone unboxing a Windows PC — or a Mac or Linux machine, for that matter — will be playing music, games or video almost immediately. That means integrating the necessary hardware for processing inputs, outputs and codecs. There are a variety of ways you can achieve that, but advancements in die sizes and chip design in general mean that what once required an entire card can be compressed into a single chip on your motherboard. If you've ever seen a mysterious Realtek Audio reference in the Windows Device Manager, that's the sort of chip we're talking about. Other chipmakers exist, but Realtek is surprisingly commonplace on Windows PCs.
Sound cards also used to be vital for microphone inputs and 3.5mm speaker outputs, but no more. Those have also been integrated into motherboards, and in many circumstances, they've become irrelevant. High-quality audio (including lossless) can easily be delivered over USB 3.x, DisplayPort, Wi-Fi or HDMI. When more compression and a little lag are acceptable, there's Bluetooth. A 24-bit, 192kHz Dolby Atmos stream in Dolby TrueHD lossless only consumes about 18 Mbps, a fraction of the 5 Gbps bandwidth USB 3.0 is capable of, never mind USB4 or Wi-Fi 7.
As if this weren't enough, there are business- and design-related incentives to move audio hardware out of your PC case. Number one is space. Laptops and handheld PCs obviously have little room to begin with, especially with never-ending competition to make devices thinner and lighter. In desktop tower PCs, much of the case may already be filled by a gigantic graphics card and its cooling systems. Any redundant cards are just going to increase power consumption and restrict airflow.
For professional audio, the inside of a PC is also a relatively unfriendly place, since all of the surrounding components can potentially introduce signal interference. It is possible to provide enough shielding, as the continued sale of internal sound cards points to. But for optimal results and more convenient interfaces, it's just logical to keep most pro sound gear out on your desk.
When a sound card actually makes sense
With most consumer-level audio taken care of, the one area where sound cards reign supreme is in tandem with professional audio interfaces. These setups tend to support even higher fidelity than integrated chips, which may be required for mastering and production. And as we just noted, they enable more convenient controls with less risk of interference. If you're going to connect mics, pedals, guitars and keyboards to your PC on a regular basis, it would be ridiculous not to put those inputs and their knobs out in the open.
There is one aspect to modern sound cards that both pros and media connoisseurs can potentially benefit from: headphone amplification. Your motherboard may lack the power to handle high-impedance headphones, which offer extra precision for those who need it or simply enjoy it. And with an external add-on, you can potentially switch high-end headphones from device to device in a matter of seconds.
The gist is that if you're just trying to listen to music or play games, there's no real incentive to splurge on a sound card. With the right set of speakers or headphones, there's usually nothing stopping you from getting spatial or lossless audio from your PC's built-in equipment. It's only wealthy purists or people aiming to be the next Hans Zimmer or Aphex Twin who need to step up their tech.

And with an external add-on, you can potentially switch high-end headphones from device to device in a matter of seconds.
The gist is that if you're just trying to listen to music or play games, there's no real incentive to splurge on a sound card. With the right set of speakers or headphones, there's usually nothing stopping you from getting spatial or lossless audio from your PC's built-in equipment. It's only wealthy purists or people aiming to be the next Hans Zimmer or Aphex Twin who need to step up their tech.

title_en: The popular Apple features you won't be getting with the iPhone Duo
title_fa: The popular Apple features you won't be getting with the iPhone Duo
excerpt_en: The iPhone Duo lacks a few features we're used to seeing on other iPhones.
excerpt_fa: The iPhone Duo lacks a few features we're used to seeing on other iPhones.
content_en:
The popular Apple features you won't be getting with the iPhone Duo
Switching to a foldable requires some sacrifices.
Smartphone users eyeing the new iPhone Duo may be enraptured by its matte-finish inner folding display and slick software redesigned around that experience. It's certainly the most exciting Apple device in a decade or more, but Apple's first foldable phone is not without its compromises. On the Android side of the fence, foldable owners have spent years adapting to the sacrifices that come with a bleeding edge device, and it turns out Apple wasn't able to fully overcome any of them. Of course, the Duo is less durable than the more traditional iPhone 18 Pro that was released alongside it, but that's far from the only way it falls short. For some people, losing a few features in exchange for a folding display is worth it, but some of those losses will be a dealbreaker for others.
Apple's current iPhone lineup is its most diverse in recent memory, and you shouldn't feel compelled to buy the Duo when another model might make more sense for your needs. From cameras that can't quite compete to a lack of FaceID, here are the main iPhone features you'll miss out on with an iPhone Duo.
iPhone Duo ditches FaceID and Camera Control button
The biggest loss you'll feel when switching from a traditional iPhone to the Duo is the latter's lack of a FaceID array for facial recognition. You'll authenticate with fingerprints or passwords only. If you've grown accustomed to FaceID, which pretty much always works as long as your face is somewhere in front of the screen, losing that option could be a major blow. When unlocking your phone, making purchases and logging into apps requires fiddling with a finicky fingerprint sensor every time, it can become aggravating.
On the other hand, some users still miss the older iPhones with TouchID. Maybe your face doesn't play nice with FaceID for whatever reason. Maybe you just prefer the tactility of a fingerprint sensor. Apple placed the Duo's TouchID sensor in the power button, a similar implementation to that found on foldables from Samsung and other vendors.
A feature some may not miss on the iPhone Duo is the Camera Control button found on the side rail of other iPhones. It's a neat piece of kit, with a two-stage shutter and a capacitive control that allows you to change camera settings on the fly, but it seems to have gone over with some users about as well as the infamous butterfly keyboard on late 2010s MacBooks. In other words, it's innovative and cool from a tech perspective but often frustrating to use in practice.
However, if you're one of those iPhone users who swears by the Camera Control button, this loss will sting. Combined with the Duo's less capable cameras, the lack of a Camera Control button suggests that Apple sees the Duo as a media consumption device rather than a creative tool (an impression further advanced by the phone's lack of true multi-window multitasking).
The iPhone Duo's cameras leave a lot to be desired
Other major losses can be found in the iPhone Duo's camera department, ironic for a phone with so many cameras. There are three camera arrays on the iPhone Duo: the main pair of shooters on the back, the Dynamic Island selfie shooter on the front display and the under-display camera on the folding interior display which Apple is branding a FaceTime camera. Each of these systems is compromised in a major way compared to the iPhone 18 Pro's camera innovations.
Starting with the main camera array, the Duo is aptly fitted with two lenses on its back platter. It carries the two 48-megapixel wide and ultrawide modules found on its slab-shaped siblings, but lacks the periscope telephoto lens they offer. And that incredibly cool-looking mechanical aperture, icing on the iPhone 18 Pro's cake, won't be found here, nor will its LiDAR scanner for better nighttime photography. The selfie camera on the cover display is a 12-megapixel letdown compared to the iPhone 18 Pro's aptly implemented 18-megapixel self-shooter. As discussed above, it also lacks the FaceID face-scanning array.
Even on the software side, the Duo is a camera downgrade. Apple announced new Pro Controls for the iPhone 18 Pro. Users can adjust shutter speed, aperture and more, making the 18 Pro a more useful camera for professionals. Those controls are absent on the Duo. So, too, are ProRAW shots which work better in professional photo editing software, as well as spatial photo and video — not a big deal if you don't own a VR headset, but Vision Pro owners may want to consider it.
An under-display FaceTime camera
Last but certainly not least in terms of camera downgrades, the under-display FaceTime camera found on the inner display is almost certainly going to be a dog's breakfast. Apple has declined to tell anyone how many megapixels it is, which is not a great sign. We need look no further than Cupertino's largest competitor, Samsung, which used under-display cameras in the Galaxy Z Fold 4 and carried the feature forward for several generations.
The benefit of using under-display tech was always a completely uninterrupted image with no ugly "hole-punch" lens to ruin it, but it came at the cost of picture quality. Every phone that has ever had an under-display camera has failed to overcome the fact that you're putting a layer of pixels between you and the lens, and the results have been predictably awful. There's no reason to believe Apple has solved that issue, which is why they're not calling it a selfie camera but rather a FaceTime camera.
For many users, none of these tradeoffs will be particularly hard to deal with. If you're only snapping photos for personal use and social media, you'll hardly notice the lack of a periscope zoom lens or a few more megapixels of resolution in your selfies, and you probably weren't using the Camera Control on your current iPhone to begin with. The lack of FaceID might be jarring at first, but you'll quickly accustom yourself...

title_en: How the iPhone Duo will improve your group selfies
title_fa: How the iPhone Duo will improve your group selfies
excerpt_en: The iPhone Duo's foldable form factor allows for more placement options, but there are also new camera features you should know about.
excerpt_fa: The iPhone Duo's foldable form factor allows for more placement options, but there are also new camera features you should know about.
content_en:
How the iPhone Duo will improve your group selfies
No more propping your phone up and trying to beat the timer to get in the picture.
It was inevitable that Apple would hype every new camera trick with the iPhone Duo, no matter that Samsung and others have been doing similar things for years. One thing that wasn't so expected was how hard it would lean into group selfies. Its September event devoted at least a minute or two to the topic — which might not seem like much, but given that the Duo was just one product on the slate, that's saying something about what Apple thinks will sell.
There is some merit to the attention, since iPhone owners have had relatively little flexibility in group selfies until now. Even on the iPhone 18 Pro, the front-facing Center Stage camera is limited to 18 megapixels. You can get 48 megapixels with one of the rear cameras, but of course those are less than ideal for group shots you need to participate in. At most, you can find an object to prop your phone on, frame the shot and hope your timer lasts long enough for you (and everyone else) to get a proper pose in.
The Duo, shipping on October 23, aims to fix these deficiencies through the combination of a foldable form factor and a couple of new iOS 27 features. It's questionable how often people will really take advantage of these, especially with a $2,000 entry price — but it is a glimpse at the future of iPhone photography.
Going foldable means a better sensor and better software
The ability to tent an iPhone Duo and use the 48-megapixel rear cameras shouldn't be undersold. While 18 megapixels — or just 12, on the Duo's internal Center Stage camera — is sharp enough, more megapixels can translate into sharper images or extra space for cropping. More importantly, it's always the rear sensors where Apple puts its best technology in terms of low-light sensitivity and focus tracking. Indeed, one of the smaller upgrades the company is touting is "smart" focus tracking, really a rebranding of the focus lock standalone cameras have had for some time. Once you tap on a subject, the Duo's AI systems will follow it and adjust focus on the fly, even if it temporarily leaves the frame.
There's a connection between that and the centerpiece of Apple's group selfie features: Smart Take. In theory, at least, this eliminates the need for timers by scanning for motion. When triggered, Smart Take automatically takes a snap whenever everyone freezes for a moment, the assumption being that they've adopted a new pose. This seems likely to take as many bad shots as good ones, given that people may have their eyes closed or be standing around waiting for direction. Nevertheless, it's a welcome alternative to selecting a timed shot, checking the results, then rinse and repeat.
You can find the Smart Take option in the Camera app's extended settings menu. Since iOS 27 finally lets you customize the app's controls — tap the circles button in the lower-right corner, then Edit — you should also be able to have a Smart Take button permanently at the ready, if you somehow find yourself taking group selfies on a regular basis. Naturally, this is useful for solo selfies as well; it's just that coordinated group shots are often the most difficult, as any pro wedding photographer knows.
The other big software addition is Duo Preview. When activated during a shot, this displays a real-time preview on the front screen, allowing the subjects to see themselves and make their own pose adjustments. Expect this to be a double-edged sword. Some people will inevitably ham things up, or do what they think works instead of what you actually want. Still, this is undeniably a step forward, to the point that some candybar iPhone owners may feel a little jealous.
You can expect a few limitations
There are some flaws in Apple's first-generation foldable selfies, beginning with the fact that there's no telephoto lens. Admittedly, most group shots are best taken with a wide or even ultra-wide lens. One of the chief rules of good composition, however, is to fill the frame with your subject(s). Sometimes you may not be able to sit your Duo close enough to make that happen.
Another issue is handheld selfies. You're encouraged to open the Duo all the way and flip it around to get those 48-megapixel cameras, but the grip needed seems a little awkward, mostly because of the thin bezels on the front display. It could be tough to get a good handle without accidentally triggering touchscreen commands. To Apple's credit, though, this mode automatically brings all of the Camera app's controls to the front, so there's no blind shooting involved.
A big concern for some people with group selfies might be the vulnerability of a Duo left standing by itself. On top of the theft risk, we'll have to see how stable the Duo is in real-world situations. At 8.96 ounces, it's light enough to be tipped over by the wind or a nearby bump. Meanwhile, Apple's notion that some group shots should be taken with the front display touching the ground is going to be a non-starter for many users, probably, unless perhaps you buy a case that creates a protective lip. The Duo's Ceramic Shield 2 glass may be scratch-resistant, but no display is scratchproof.

title_en: How to improve your iPhone's call quality
title_fa: How to improve your iPhone's call quality
excerpt_en: Your iPhone should handle calls reliably, but if you can't hear the other person or calls aren't stable, it's time to run through a few fixes.
excerpt_fa: Your iPhone should handle calls reliably, but if you can't hear the other person or calls aren't stable, it's time to run through a few fixes.
content_en:
How to improve your iPhone's call quality
When calls drops or sound terrible, here's what to do.
When you're not using your iPhone as a music player, camera or gaming platform, you might actually use it as a phone. And when you do, call quality matters. If calls sound muffled or metallic, cut out intermittently or are drowned by background noise, you can take steps to fix the problems.
Most of the time, the causes are poor signal strength, outdated carrier settings or physical barriers like walls or metallic veneers on glass.
What you can try during the call
First, check your volume and speaker output. The volume might simply be turned down, or you might not have turned speaker mode on. Next, glance at the signal bars. If those are low, move toward a window or more open space.
You might not have noticed that you have the option to adjust the voice mode during a call. Voice Isolation is available on the iPhone XR/XS and newer, as long as you have iOS 16.4 or later. It uses machine learning to block environmental noise, so your voice sounds more audible to the other person.
To activate it during a call, swipe down from the top-right to open Control Center and tap the small Phone Controls banner at the top of the screen. Then under Audio & Video, select Voice Isolation from the available options in the Mic Mode section. You can also choose Automatic, which has your phone adjust for what's best.
Of course, since these options apply to your voice, their enhancements only apply for the person you're speaking to. If you're having trouble hearing the person on the other end of the call and they also have an iPhone, ask them to try this option (as well as the others discussed here, if their calls always sound poor).
Set your device up for call success
Get a better cellular connection
If the nearest cellular tower is congested, your iPhone may connect to a more distant tower with a weaker signal. It could also cling onto a weak connection even when a stronger one is available. If your call drops or the sound is bad, end the call, then swipe down from the top-right to open Control Center. There, toggle Airplane Mode on, wait 10 seconds and toggle it off again. This forces your device to reconnect to the cellular network, hopefully with a stronger signal.
Switch to Wi-Fi Calling
With Wi-Fi Calling, your call is handled by a Wi-Fi connection instead of a potentially weak cellular network. It's a great option if cell reception in parts of your home is poor. To enable it, open Settings > Apps > Phone, tap Wi-Fi Calling, then enable Wi-Fi Calling on This iPhone. Wi-Fi calling should hand off to your cellular network if you leave Wi-Fi range mid-call, but this isn't perfect, so you might experience drops.
Update your software
Apple regularly patches issues that may impact call quality. Check Settings > General > Software Update to make sure iOS is current. You should also check your for carrier settings updates in Settings > General > About. If an update's available, a prompt should appear within 15-seconds. Tap Update.
Everything else you can try to improve your iPhone calls
Restart your phone
The oldest trick in the book still works to fix a lot of issues, so try restarting your iPhone if you haven't in a while. If your iPhone uses a SIM card, pop the tray out with a paper clip to check for dust or a loose fit (while the phone is turned off).
Physical checks
Test your microphone by recording yourself using the Voice Memos app. If that playback sounds clear, you know it's not a hardware problem.
Clean the speaker grill and earpiece with a soft brush, and try a call without a case since thick or metal cases can interfere with antenna performance. Also, try using speakerphone during a call to see if that makes a difference.
Headsets and AirPods
Bluetooth headphones, including AirPods, share the 2.4GHz band with a multitude of other devices including mice, keyboards, microwaves and baby monitors. This network congestion can degrade call quality. Try making calls without your headphones and see if the audio is any clearer. Or if you've never made a call with headphones, try them to see if they perform better than the internal mic.
Hardware faults
Some iPhone 12 and 12 Pro models had high earpiece failure rates, which Apple addressed in a now-closed service program. Older iPhones with Intel modems (iPhone XR, XS or 11) may also have weaker signal strength. You can contact Apple if you think a hardware issue is causing your problem, but this will likely result in having to come into the store for a paid session.

title_en: Google froze its open source bug bounty program due to a ‘significant rise’ in AI submissions
title_fa: Google froze its open source bug bounty program due to a ‘significant rise’ in AI submissions
excerpt_en: AI slop seems to be overwhelming bug bounty programs.
excerpt_fa: AI slop seems to be overwhelming bug bounty programs.
content_en:
Blaming a “significant rise” in AI submissions, Google has paused its open source bug bounty program until next year.
Last year, TechCrunch reported that cybersecurity experts were warning of that AI slop posed a serious risk to bug bounty programs. Looks like that’s the issue confronting Google’s Open Source Software Vulnerability Rewards Program, where researchers were rewarded for finding vulnerabilities in the company’s open source software.
In posts on X and the program website, Google said the bug bounty program was paused as of October 1, with a promise to provide “an update” in the first quarter of 2027. According to Tom’s Hardware, Google engineers and open source maintainers were overwhelmed by reports that were invalid or contained hallucinations.
“This pause is due to a significant rise in automated submissions, the vast majority of which are not valid,” the company said.
In the meantime, participants are encouraged to consider Google’s other bug bounty programs.

title_en: Can ‘super intelligence’ and a non-binding safety pact solve AI’s image problem?
title_fa: Can ‘super intelligence’ and a non-binding safety pact solve AI’s image problem?
excerpt_en: On Equity, we discussed the Trump administration's attempts to rebrand AI.
excerpt_fa: On Equity, we discussed the Trump administration's attempts to rebrand AI.
content_en:
President Donald Trump hosted many of the biggest names in artificial intelligence this week — in part to announce that the U.S. government isn’t calling it artificial intelligence anymore. Now it’s super intelligence.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed the motivation behind the meeting and what effect it might have on the AI industry. We were all pretty skeptical that the “Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities” that the executives signed will amount to much, especially since — as Sean noted — it’s “deeply non-binding,” at least from a legal prospective. (Instead, Trump said he considers it “morally binding.”)
Kirsten suggested that the meeting’s real significance may have been as “a rebranding effort around AI.” (An effort that continued this weekend with Trump’s announcement of a new Super Intelligence Force.) For her, the big message was, “AI is going to kill us, it’s scary, it is going to take jobs — but super intelligence is not.”
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.
Anthony Ha: Officially, by order of the president of the United States, it’s not artificial intelligence anymore, it’s super intelligence. We were talking about this last week, because this is something [Trump has] been hinting at — he doesn’t do hints, he’s been saying [it] for a while. But now it’s signed into executive order. If you’re an official U.S. representative, you are supposed to say super intelligence, not artificial intelligence.
And this was also part of this broader announcement around AI safety, which I think is both interesting for this pact that was announced, but also the fact that it happened at all. It seemed to have come together fairly quickly, because just two weeks ago, a week ago, President Trump was saying, “We don’t need any of this, we need to lead in AI, we can’t constrain it in any way, we don’t need any regulation, anyone who’s saying that there’s any danger from AI is essentially a Chinese or Democratic plant.” And yet all these AI CEOs got together with him earlier this week and signed this pact.
Kirsten Korosec: Leading up to that, we should say, not only was there pushback on regulation, and we can talk about whether this executive order even does any of that — I would say no, there’s a little bit of theater there — but the important and interesting thing is that just days ago, Anthropic was really in the doghouse, if you will, in terms of what was happening behind the scenes with President Trump.
That all changed when [Anthropic CEO] Dario Amodei was invited to a 10 p.m. dinner. He had this sit-down, and then just days later, we had this luncheon, and at this luncheon, we have pretty much every tech power broker from every major tech company that exists. So Mark Zuckerberg was there, Jeff Bezos was there, Elon Musk was there, Dario of course was there, they were all there.
I’m wondering if any of you watched the press conference that happened afterwards, which there’s been many, many memes about, because of the interesting, funny behavior when you bring a bunch of tech CEOs together.
But I guess my bigger question for both of you is: What does this all mean? And does it mean anything?
Sean O’Kane: How much time do you have? First off, sure, they had dinner, Trump and Dario. If you read the Time magazine interview that Trump just did, your guess is as good as mine as to how informed he was that that dinner was even going to be happening, which is a strange reality to live in, but it’s just the one we inhabit.
I will also say one other thing that makes me skeptical — surprise, surprise — of how repaired the relationship is between the administration and Anthropic, is that for as much as there are clearly people trying to put those two groups together, the Defense Department is still very adamant that Anthropic is terrible and woke and and a national security risk. Emil Michael goes off on Anthropic every other day on X, it seems. I think there’s still some distance there despite Dario showing up to this thing.
As far as the agreement and all of that, let’s be real, they misspelled the United States on the agreement that they all signed. It is also just deeply non-binding. I mean, it is completely voluntary. I think my favorite aspect about it was that Trump described it as quote “morally binding,” which is just a level of abstraction and terminology that I’ve never heard of before.
Anthony: In terms of Anthropic and their relationship with the Trump administration, there’s been a sort of a lot of reporting, especially during that big blow up with the Defense Department, that different parts of the White House had different relationships with Anthropic. The Treasury Secretary seemed to be a big fan, whereas the Defense Department — definitely not big fans, or at least unhappy with some of the conditions that Anthropic were trying to put on the use of their technology.
In that sense, it feels like nothing has necessarily changed. There are people in the White House who want to use Anthropic’s technology, want them involved in these decisions, and others who really, really, really, really don’t.
In terms of the agreement, it seems not super meaningful. What is meaningful is just the fact that they felt that this was something worth doing. As indicated by the fact that they misspelled United States, it seemed like they rushed to put all of this together. [But] the fact that this kind of gesture was needed seems significant, even if I don’t think the agreement itself is going to lead to any major changes.
Kirsten: I do think that there was one important thing that happened. And to me, this is the point of it, which was a rebranding exercise around AI. “AI is going to kill us, it’s scary, it is going to take jobs, but super intelligence is not.” This isn’t my personal belief. To me, that was the message.

title_en: Prick’s theatrical industrial punk is perfect for spooky season
title_fa: Prick’s theatrical industrial punk is perfect for spooky season
excerpt_en: While deep in the recording process for The Downward Spiral, Trent Reznor lent some of his production talents to old friend Kevin McMahon, from the new wave band Lucky Pierre (which Reznor was briefly a member of). While Reznor is only credited as the producer on four tracks off...
excerpt_fa: While deep in the recording process for The Downward Spiral, Trent Reznor lent some of his production talents to old friend Kevin McMahon, from the new wave band Lucky Pierre (which Reznor was briefly a member of). While Reznor is only credited as the producer on four tracks off...
content_en:
While deep in the recording process for The Downward Spiral, Trent Reznor lent some of his production talents to old friend Kevin McMahon, from the new wave band Lucky Pierre (which Reznor was briefly a member of). While Reznor is only credited as the producer on four tracks off Prick’s self-titled debut record, his fingerprints are all over it. But McMahon also can’t suppress his inner theater kid, which also gives the songs the sort of glammy flamboyance found on T. Rex records. Prick embraces the inherent theatricality of goth in a way that Nine Inch Nails never did.
Prick’s theatrical industrial punk is perfect for spooky season
If Trent Reznor studied musical theater instead of computer engineering NIN might have sounded like Prick.
Prick’s theatrical industrial punk is perfect for spooky season
If Trent Reznor studied musical theater instead of computer engineering NIN might have sounded like Prick.
Opener “Communiqué” is a fuzzy blast of simple punk riffs with electronic sprinklings on top. McMahon’s vocals occasionally detour from the half-spoken verses that sound borrowed from a musical to full-throated Al Jourgensen-esque screams. The rough-around-the-edges production and focus on live instrumentation feel like a prototype for what Reznor would eventually revisit on With Teeth.
But it’s the second track, “Riverhead” where Reznor’s influences fully rear their head (even though he is not actually credited as the producer). The vocal melodies swerve like Outside- and Earthling-era Bowie around guitars that buzz with all the digital charr of the Broken EP. Then, around the three-minute mark, comes the breakdown. It slowly builds with layers of electronic drums, mechanical chords, and loping synthetic-sounding guitar melodies. The entire back chunk could easily have been a Downward Spiral or even The Fragile B-side.
These moments of richly layered production, though, are almost always immediately undermined, as with the sloppy garage-punk intro of “Tough”.
It’s these moments that make Prick so charming. It’s a serious record, but it never takes itself too seriously. McMahon isn’t afraid to get goofy (“Pink panties, blue panties, yellow panties. I’m gonna wrap around your nose, oh panty-ho-hose” he sings on “Other People”) and over-the-top with his vocal performances. He’s willing to let the guitar drift out of time, the bass strings rattle, and revels in industrial lo-fi.
“Animal” is perhaps the best-known track from the album, its video having received at least some MTV airplay. It combines backward melodic samples reminiscent of “Closer” and follows a similar lyrical theme:
Consent is all I need
To bring out the savage in me
Your scent is all I need
To bring out the animal in me
But where “Closer” opts for slinky disco sleaze, “Animal” is all raw shouted desire.
“I Apologize” is the most scatter-brained track on the album, and for that reason, one of my favorites. It opens with awkward whip-crack-like percussion and McMahon singing slightly flat and unaffected, before briefly taking off into a jangly new wave verse that quickly morphs into a hard-rock stop in the chorus. But that’s short-lived as well. The second verse is all “Space Oddity”-era Bowie acoustic strums, then there’s a solo that sounds like an arcade machine on the verge of meltdown. That then drops into a Ministry-esque dirge of layered guitars and screams. The song then returns to the chorus, but keeps adding elements until it’s stuffed to capacity and collapses on itself.
Prick’s self-titled record has plenty in common with other ‘90s industrial acts. But McMahon is clearly having a lot more fun than many of his contemporaries, and that helps elevate it above the myriad Nine Inch Nails wannabes out there.
Prick is available on most major streaming services, including Apple Music, Spotify, Qobuz, Deezer, and YouTube Music.

title_en: The upcoming touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro is reportedly 'significantly lighter'
title_fa: The upcoming touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro is reportedly 'significantly lighter'
excerpt_en: The high-end laptop is still expected to make its debut by next month.
excerpt_fa: The high-end laptop is still expected to make its debut by next month.
content_en:
The upcoming touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro is reportedly 'significantly lighter'
The high-end laptop is still expected to make its debut by next month.
Not only will the next MacBook Pro have OLED technology and a touchscreen display, it will reportedly weigh less. As reported by Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, the upcoming MacBook Pro might be "significantly lighter" thanks to Apple reworking the laptop's interiors by miniaturizing parts and rearranging components.
While we're not sure how the touchscreen MacBook Pro's internals will be arranged, we last heard that it will feature the existing higher-end M5 chips, instead of the upcoming M7 chips that are expected to debut in early 2027. Gurman reiterated that the touchscreen MacBook Pro with OLED should be coming out next month, alongside the first iPad mini to similarly feature OLED. As for the current MacBook Pro models, the laptop starts at 3.4 pounds with the 14-inch model and can weigh up to 4.7 pounds for the 16-inch version.
The soon-to-be-revealed MacBook Pro with touchscreen and OLED tech could represent a major hardware milestone under John Ternus, who recently took over as Apple's CEO. Unlike his predecessor who was known for supply chain and logistics prowess, Ternus could bring back more of a focus on product design, especially with his previous experience as a hardware engineer, according to Gurman. Gurman added that one of the CEO's first priorities was to rebuild its design teams, which also now report directly to Ternus.

title_en: Five iPhone 18 Pro features you'll want to try the second you unbox it
title_fa: Five iPhone 18 Pro features you'll want to try the second you unbox it
excerpt_en: The iPhone 18 Pro doesn't have a super long list of improvements, but these upgrades are still worth a try.
excerpt_fa: The iPhone 18 Pro doesn't have a super long list of improvements, but these upgrades are still worth a try.
content_en:
Five iPhone 18 Pro features you’ll want to try the second you unbox it
From variable aperture to faster charging, here’s what to test first.
The iPhone 18 Pro is finally here, and while it might not seem as exciting as the new iPhone Duo, there's plenty to try out once you take it out of the box. This year, Apple is providing even more control in the Camera app. The camera's main lens with a variable aperture opens up new possibilities for photography, as do the new Photographic Styles.
Not only that, but the Dynamic Island is smaller and charging your iPhone is much faster. If you have an iPhone 18 Pro or plan on getting one, check out these highlights first.
Play with the camera's new variable aperture
The 48-megapixel main camera is the first on an iPhone to feature variable aperture. The lens has six blades that physically open and close, just like on a DSLR camera. This offers greater control over the amount of light in the scene as well as the depth of field. You get four settings in the Camera app: f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8 and f/4. Try shooting the same subject at each and compare them — you'll notice differences in lighting, noise and background.
At f/1.48, the sensor lets in more light and blurs the background more, which is perfect for that photo in a dimly lit restaurant. Switch to f/4 to reduce the aperture; you'll have less light, but everyone in the photo will look sharper. It's perfect for group photos or landscapes. The smaller aperture also creates a cool starburst effect on bright lights.
You can find the aperture controls by tapping the six-dot button in the Camera app. But remember: this control only works on the main lens, in 1x and 2x modes. Other lenses still have a fixed aperture, just like before.
Go through the new Pro camera controls
Aperture control isn't the only new feature in the Camera app on iPhone 18 Pro. Apple has also added a bunch of other manual controls for the first time — the kind of features you used to find only in third-party apps. You can also adjust the shutter speed, focus, and white balance. A slow shutter speed turns car headlights into streaks, while locking white balance stops skin tones from shifting as you walk between rooms with different lighting.
All these controls are located inside the same six-dot button, along with the aperture setting. What's great is that you can customize the Camera app for easier access to your favorite controls. Press and hold the controls at the top of the Camera app, then drag the ones you want to keep there at all times.
Adjust grain and texture in Photographic Styles
Photographic Styles were introduced with the iPhone 13, but the feature has changed quite a bit since then. If you're not familiar with them, Photographic Styles let you change how a photo looks —from contrast to shadows and colors — by adjusting only specific layers of the image, unlike a basic filter. And for those with an iPhone 18 Pro, there are two new controls available: grain and texture.
Take a photo with any of the cameras on your new iPhone, then open the editing menu and tap Styles to see the new options. Select Customize, then go to the Texture tab to adjust. Here, you can soften skin tones without affecting the rest of the image, add some glow or apply a film effect to the highlights. If you like that old-school grainy effect, that's possible, too. Messing around with all these new styles is a great way to give your photos a nicer look.
Try out the new Dynamic Island
One of the coolest features of modern iPhones is the Dynamic Island. Apple took a hardware limitation and turned it into a cool iOS feature: a simple cutout around the front-facing camera becomes an area for showing useful information. On the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple has made the Dynamic Island smaller, so you'll see more of your content when it's not active. And when Dynamic Island is in use, it can do even more now.
Dynamic Island now shows not just one, but up to three Live Activities at once. This means you can control your music, check the progress of a timer and keep track of the score of a sporting event all at the same time. Everything works just like on previous models, where you press and hold on each Live Activity in the Dynamic Island to expand it. Any apps that already work with the Dynamic Island can take advantage of these improvements.
Plug it in for a fast charge
Apple says the batteries in the new iPhones last longer, and while that's true, they won't last forever. But when it's time to charge your iPhone 18 Pro, you can do it much faster than before. It charges from 0 to 50 percent in about 15 minutes, or 30 minutes if you're using a MagSafe charger. Forgetting to charge your iPhone overnight will no longer be a problem.
There's a catch, though. To get the most out of fast charging, you need the right power adapter. Five iPhone 18 Pro features you’ll want to try the second you unbox it
From variable aperture to faster charging, here’s what to test first.
The iPhone 18 Pro is finally here, and while it might not seem as exciting as the new iPhone Duo, there's plenty to try out once you take it out of the box. This year, Apple is providing even more control in the Camera app. The camera's main lens with a variable aperture opens up new possibilities for photography, as do the new Photographic Styles.
Not only that, but the Dynamic Island is smaller and charging your iPhone is much faster. If you have an iPhone 18 Pro or plan on getting one, check out these highlights first.
Play with the camera's new variable aperture
The 48-megapixel main camera is the first on an iPhone to feature variable aperture. The lens has six blades that physically open and close, just like on a DSLR camera. This offers greater control over the amount of light in the scene as well as the depth of field. You get four settings in the Camera app: f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8 and f/4. Try shooting the same subject at each and compare them — you'll notice differences in lighting, noise and background.
At f/1.48, the sensor lets in more light and blurs the background more, which is perfect for that photo in a dimly lit restaurant. Switch to f/4 to reduce the aperture; you'll have less light, but everyone in the photo will look sharper. It's perfect for group photos or landscapes. The smaller aperture also creates a cool starburst effect on bright lights.
You can find the aperture controls by tapping the six-dot button in the Camera app. But remember: this control only works on the main lens, in 1x and 2x modes. Other lenses still have a fixed aperture, just like before.
Go through the new Pro camera controls
Aperture control isn't the only new feature in the Camera app on iPhone 18 Pro. Apple has also added a bunch of other manual controls for the first time — the kind of features you used to find only in third-party apps. You can also adjust the shutter speed, focus, and white balance. A slow shutter speed turns car headlights into streaks, while locking white balance stops skin tones from shifting as you walk between rooms with different lighting.
All these controls are located inside the same six-dot button, along with the aperture setting. What's great is that you can customize the Camera app for easier access to your favorite controls. Press and hold the controls at the top of the Camera app, then drag the ones you want to keep there at all times.
Adjust grain and texture in Photographic Styles
Photographic Styles were introduced with the iPhone 13, but the feature has changed quite a bit since then. If you're not familiar with them, Photographic Styles let you change how a photo looks —from contrast to shadows and colors — by adjusting only specific layers of the image, unlike a basic filter. And for those with an iPhone 18 Pro, there are two new controls available: grain and texture.
Take a photo with any of the cameras on your new iPhone, then open the editing menu and tap Styles to see the new options. Select Customize, then go to the Texture tab to adjust. Here, you can soften skin tones without affecting the rest of the image, add some glow or apply a film effect to the highlights. If you like that old-school grainy effect, that's possible, too. Messing around with all these new styles is a great way to give your photos a nicer look.
Try out the new Dynamic Island
One of the coolest features of modern iPhones is the Dynamic Island. Apple took a hardware limitation and turned it into a cool iOS feature: a simple cutout around the front-facing camera becomes an area for showing useful information. On the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple has made the Dynamic Island smaller, so you'll see more of your content when it's not active. And when Dynamic Island is in use, it can do even more now.
Dynamic Island now shows not just one, but up to three Live Activities at once. This means you can control your music, check the progress of a timer and keep track of the score of a sporting event all at the same time. Everything works just like on previous models, where you press and hold on each Live Activity in the Dynamic Island to expand it. Any apps that already work with the Dynamic Island can take advantage of these improvements.
Plug it in for a fast charge
Apple says the batteries in the new iPhones last longer, and while that's true, they won't last forever. But when it's time to charge your iPhone 18 Pro, you can do it much faster than before.
